front.title: Forward Error Correction for Media over QUIC

abstract.t: This document specifies a mechanism for transmitting Forward Error Correction (FEC) repair data alongside source media in Media over QUIC (MoQ) sessions. It defines catalog-based signaling of FEC configuration, including a derived RaptorQ Object Transmission Information that needs no in-session messages. It also defines conventions for repair track naming, the format of repair objects, and two block profiles that fix how source symbols and FEC blocks are formed and identified: an ISO/IEC 23008-1 profile for tracks packaged as MPEG Media Transport Protocol (MMTP) packets, and an object profile for tracks packaged as Low Overhead Media Container (LOC) or Common Media Application Format (CMAF) objects. It fully specifies two FEC schemes: the systematic Reed-Solomon code over GF(2^8) of ISO/IEC 23008-10, which is mandatory to implement, and RaptorQ (RFC 6330), which is optional. An algorithm registry provides extension points for additional schemes. FEC enables receivers to recover from packet loss without retransmission latency. The MMTP profile is designed for compatibility with ATSC 3.0 (A/331) and ARIB STD-B60 broadcast systems.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Media over QUIC (MoQ) provides a publish/subscribe transport for real-time media. While QUIC provides reliable delivery through retransmission, the latency incurred by retransmission can be unacceptable for ultra-low-latency (ULL) applications such as live sports, gaming, and interactive broadcasts.

Forward Error Correction (FEC) enables receivers to recover lost packets using redundant repair data, without waiting for retransmissions. This is particularly valuable in wireless environments where burst packet loss is common.
This document defines:

ol.li: A catalog extension carrying the complete FEC configuration, which is authoritative for MoQ receivers

A normative derivation of the parameters of the Reed-Solomon code, and of the RaptorQ Object Transmission Information (OTI), from the catalog fields and the Repair FEC Payload ID of each block, so that catalog-only receivers (including multicast and sessionless receivers) can fully configure their decoders
A naming convention for repair tracks

The format of repair objects containing FEC symbols, and two block profiles: iso-ssbg1-v1, which forms source symbols and FEC blocks from MPEG Media Transport Protocol (MMTP) packets as Annex C of does, and moq-object-v1, which forms them from whole MoQ objects
Interleaving strategies to protect against burst loss

A compatibility statement for ATSC 3.0 MMTP sessions (Section 12). ARIB STD-B60 carriage of MMTP-packaged tracks uses the in-band AL-FEC signaling of Section 8.3, and its Section 10 covers ARIB STD-B60 ingest.

section.t: The mechanism protects tracks whose packaging a block profile admits. Under iso-ssbg1-v1 it protects MMTP-packaged tracks , and Section 7.3 specifies the protected source symbol. Under moq-object-v1 it protects tracks packaged as Low Overhead Media Container (LOC) or Common Media Application Format (CMAF) , and Section 7.6 specifies the protected source symbols. Section 13 compares the two ways to protect CMAF content.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
Source Track: A MoQ track carrying media data (e.g., video, audio).

Repair Track: A MoQ track carrying FEC repair symbols for a corresponding source track, in repair objects whose form the source track's block profile fixes (Section 7.1): MMTP FEC repair packets ( Section C.4.3) under iso-ssbg1-v1, and a Repair FEC Payload ID with one symbol under moq-object-v1 (Section 7.6.3). Under iso-ssbg1-v1, the layer-0 repair track (Section 6.3) carries the FEC repair flow ( 3.1.9) that an ISO AL-FEC message names for the source track's FEC encoded flow (3.1.7); further repair layers (Section 6.3) and a keyframe overlay (Section 6.4) are repair tracks that only the catalog declares ( Section 8.3).

Source Block: A sequence of SSB_length source symbols, 1 <= SSB_length <= K, over which FEC encoding is performed, where SSB_length is the block's source symbol count (Section 7.1) and K the track's sourceSymbols (Section 5.1); under iso-ssbg1-v1, the ISO source symbol block (3.1.34), generated from a source packet block (3.1.32). Under raptorq, a block of SSB_length source symbols is an source block whose K, in the notation of , is SSB_length; this document's K is the catalog bound instead. The extension of that source block to K' symbols by padding ( Section 5.3.1) happens inside the encoder and the decoder and is not visible on the wire, and this document defines no K' of its own.

Source Symbol: A fixed-size unit of source data used for FEC encoding: under iso-ssbg1-v1, one FEC source packet framed as Section 7.3 specifies, and under moq-object-v1, one T-byte slice of a Protected Object Unit (Section 7.6.1).
Repair Symbol: A symbol generated by the FEC encoder that can be used to recover lost source symbols.
FEC Block: The combination of SSB_length source symbols and P repair symbols; the ISO encoding symbol block (3.1.5).

Repair Layer: One of possibly several repair tracks protecting the same source blocks of a source track, each carrying a disjoint range of the block's repair symbols (Section 6.3). All layers of a source track share one source block partition and differ only in how many repair symbols they carry. Layer 0 is the track named by repairTrack.
Layer Index: The integer repairLayer giving a layer's position in the ordered set of repair layers of one source track. Layer 0 is the base layer; enhancement layers are numbered contiguously from 1.
RS_ID Offset: The first Repair Symbol ID a layer may use; O_i for layer i (Section 6.3.2).

Keyframe Overlay: A second, independent FEC instance over a source track whose source symbols are only the fragments of Random Access Points, with its own source symbol count, its own repair symbols, and its own repair track, declared with "scope": "keyframe" (Section 6.4). An overlay is not a repair layer and carries no layer index. It is defined only under iso-ssbg1-v1.

Interleave Depth: When positive, the complete time span, in milliseconds, of one FEC source/repair packet block, signaled as interleaveDepthMs (Section 5.1); the catalog form of protection_window_time in Sections 11.2 and C.6.3. Zero is not a millisecond span: under iso-ssbg1-v1 it selects the ISO packet-count alternative, and under moq-object-v1 it is equivalent to an absent field (Section 5.1).
Object Transmission Information (OTI): Parameters required to configure a RaptorQ decoder, as defined in .

SS_ID: The 32-bit sequence number of a source symbol. Under iso-ssbg1-v1 it is carried in the Source FEC Payload ID of its FEC source packet ( Section C.5.2) and advances by one per FEC source packet. Under moq-object-v1 the FEC Source Info Property of a source object (Section 5.3) carries the SS_ID of its first source symbol, and the SS_ID advances by the object's symbol count (Section 7.6.2). It wraps modulo 2^32 (Section 7.5).

SS_Start and SSB_length: The first SS_ID of a source block and the block's source symbol count, carried in the Repair FEC Payload ID of every repair packet of the block (Section 7.1). A block is the SS_ID range [SS_Start, SS_Start + SSB_length) and is identified by its SS_Start; this document defines no block number.

Block Profile: The rules that fix how source symbols are formed from a source packet or a source object and how FEC blocks are sized, delimited and identified, named per FEC-protected source track by fec.blockProfile (Section 5.1).
Protected Object Unit: Under moq-object-v1, the bytes that one source object contributes to its FEC block: its Location, its Immutable Properties and its payload, framed as Section 7.6.1 specifies.

section.name: Protocol Overview
section.t: The protocol operates as follows (Appendix A.1 shows the exchange):

ol.li: Subscriber obtains the catalog and reads the track's fec object (Section 5), which carries the complete FEC configuration
Subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE for source track
Publisher responds with SUBSCRIBE_OK
Subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE for the repair track if FEC protection is desired (Section 6.2)
Publisher sends source objects and repair objects
Subscriber configures its decoder from the catalog fields and the Repair FEC Payload ID of each block (Sections 4.2 and 4.5) and uses repair symbols to recover any lost source symbols

section.t: The catalog is the subscriber's authoritative FEC configuration; the subscriber needs no other FEC signaling (Section 5.2).

When source objects are delivered as QUIC datagrams (unreliable), FEC recovery is the primary loss mitigation mechanism. When they are delivered on QUIC streams, QUIC retransmission recovers lost packets, and receivers MAY skip FEC decoding. Stream delivery is reliable only until a delivery timeout or a stream reset abandons an object ( Section 5.2); a receiver that holds repair symbols for the object's block can still recover it by FEC.

section.name: FEC Configuration
section.t: This section defines the FEC algorithm identifiers and the decoder parameters that constitute a track's FEC configuration, which is signaled in the catalog (Section 5.2); for RaptorQ, the full RFC 6330 Object Transmission Information is derived from the catalog fields (Section 4.2) rather than carried on the wire, and for Reed-Solomon, Section 4.4 fixes the code and its parameters are derived in the same way (Section 4.5).

section.name: FEC Algorithms
section.t: FEC algorithm values are registered in the "MoQ FEC Algorithms" registry (Section 15.2); the catalog (Section 5.1) carries the corresponding string identifiers.

RaptorQ (0x01): RaptorQ fountain code per . Can recover from loss of any symbols as long as SSB_length symbols (source or repair), plus a small decoding overhead (Section 6.3.2), are received. It is OPTIONAL (Section 4.3).

Reed-Solomon (0x02): The systematic Reed-Solomon erasure code over GF(2^8) of Clause 6, restated in Section 4.4. It recovers a block from any SSB_length of its distinct source and repair symbols. An FEC instance under it holds at most 255 source and repair symbols per block (Section 4.5). It is the mandatory-to-implement scheme (Section 4.3).

Both codes are systematic: the source symbols of a block are among its encoding symbols, so a receiver uses the source symbols it receives as they arrive. The two values correspond to the FEC code points 3 (the "6330 code") and 1 (the RS code) of Table 1, which an AL-FEC message carries in fec_code_id_for_repair_flow ( Section 8.3).

section.name: RaptorQ Object Transmission Information
section.t: An RFC 6330 decoder is configured by the Object Transmission Information (OTI): the 8-byte Common FEC OTI (Section 3.3.2 of ) and the 4-byte Scheme-Specific FEC OTI (Section 3.3.3 of ), totaling 12 bytes:
section.artwork: RaptorQ OTI { Transfer Length (40), Reserved (8), Symbol Size (16), Number of Source Blocks (8), Number of Sub-Blocks (16), Symbol Alignment (8), }
section.t: This specification does not carry the OTI on the wire. When a track's catalog fec.algorithm is "raptorq", receivers MUST construct the OTI of each FEC block from the catalog fields (Section 5.1) and the block's SSB_length, which every repair packet of the block carries (Section 7.1), under the source symbol construction of the track's block profile (Sections 7.3 and 7.6.1), as follows:

ul.li: Transfer Length: F = SSB_length x T, where SSB_length is the block's source symbol count (Section 7.1) and T is symbolSize, exact because every source symbol of either block profile is exactly T bytes. It is never computed from the cumulative size of source objects, which a receiver that has lost objects could not know, and never from sourceSymbols, which bounds SSB_length but is not the size of any particular block (Section 7.4). From this F an decoder derives that document's K as SSB_length, and from K its own K' ( Section 5.3.1).
Symbol Size: T = symbolSize.

Number of Source Blocks: Z = 1. Each FEC block of this specification is decoded as an independent RFC 6330 object containing a single source block. Blocks are identified by the SS_Start of the Repair FEC Payload ID of repair objects (Section 7.1), and source symbols are placed in them by SS_ID (Section 8.3) -- not by the RFC 6330 Z partitioning.
Number of Sub-Blocks: N = 1. Catalog-signaled sessions do not use sub-blocking (Section 7.3).
Symbol Alignment: Al = 8. symbolSize MUST be a multiple of 8.

section.t: This derivation is normative and complete: a receiver that has a track's catalog fec object requires no additional signaling to configure its decoder (Section 5.2). Its one per-block input, SSB_length, travels in the Repair FEC Payload ID of every repair packet of the block, so a receiver holding any repair symbol of a block holds the block's SSB_length.

section.name: Algorithm Requirements
section.t: Reed-Solomon is the mandatory-to-implement FEC scheme: an implementation that performs FEC decoding under this specification MUST support "reed-solomon", which Sections 4.4 and 4.5 fully specify. "raptorq" is OPTIONAL.

The MMT AL-FEC framework on which the MMTP profile of this document rests ( Annex C) requires no FEC code: it carries whichever code the AL-FEC message names by its code point, and ATSC 3.0, which applies AL-FEC to an MMTP session through that framework, requires none either ( Section 8.1.2.5; Section 12). This document therefore specifies the codes it uses. Reed-Solomon is the mandatory scheme because it is small to implement, recovers a block from exactly SSB_length of its symbols, and is a code of that framework ( code point 1). RaptorQ stays specified, code point 3, for its block size: it serves every block size this document allows. A RaptorQ block holds up to 56403 source symbols (Section 6.3.4, rule 6), while a Reed-Solomon block holds at most 255 source and repair symbols (Section 4.5). At 8 Mb/s with symbols of 1200 bytes, such a block spans at most about 300 ms of media, so the multi-second interleave windows of Section 9 need RaptorQ at that rate. A code of other than these two is outside this document until the registry below lists it.

The algorithm registry (Section 15.2) provides an extension point for additional schemes. A registered value other than "none", "raptorq" and "reed-solomon" needs a specification of its own, giving its symbol construction, parameter derivation and repair object semantics, before it can be used interoperably.

A receiver that does not implement a track's signaled fec.algorithm simply forgoes FEC protection for that track: it consumes the source track normally and does not subscribe to the repair track. Repair-track subscription is optional (Section 6.2), so an unrecognized or unimplemented algorithm is not an error. A track under "raptorq" is therefore protected only for the receivers that implement it.

section.name: Reed-Solomon Code
section.t: The "reed-solomon" algorithm is the systematic Reed-Solomon erasure code over GF(2^8) of Clause 6, to which that document assigns FEC code point 1 (its Table 1). This section restates the code, because is not freely available. If this restatement and Clause 6 differ, governs. Appendix C gives test vectors.

Field. The code works in GF(2^8) defined by the primitive polynomial x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + 1 (0x11D), the polynomial that Section 8.1 gives for m = 8. alpha is a root of that polynomial and is represented by the byte 0x02. A byte with bits b_7 (the most significant) down to b_0 represents the element b_7 alpha^7 + b_6 alpha^6 + ... + b_1 alpha + b_0. Addition is the bitwise exclusive OR of bytes, and multiplication is the product of polynomials modulo 0x11D, so alpha^8 is 0x1D. This document defines the code over GF(2^8) only.

Generator matrix. The code is generated by G = [I | A], where I is an identity matrix and A is a Cauchy matrix ( Clause 6.2 writes G = [I; A]). Row i of A belongs to the source symbol at ESI i, and column j to the repair symbol whose RS_ID is j. The entries of A are:
section.artwork: A_{i,j} = 1 / (x_i + y_j) x_i = alpha^(254 - i) y_j = alpha^j
section.t: A block that holds SSB_length source symbols and RSB_length repair symbols uses rows 0 to SSB_length - 1 and columns 0 to RSB_length - 1 of A. x_i and y_j differ whenever i + j < 254, so every entry the block uses is defined when SSB_length + RSB_length is at most 255, the bound of Clause 6.2. An entry depends on i and j alone: not on K, not on SSB_length and not on P.

Encoding. Every symbol of a block is T bytes long. Let s_i be the source symbol at ESI i (Section 8.3), for i from 0 to SSB_length - 1. The repair symbol r_j whose RS_ID is j is computed one byte position at a time, as Section 8.4 applies its code to symbols: for each byte position u from 0 to T - 1,
section.artwork: r_j[u] = sum over i < SSB_length of A_{i,j} * s_i[u]
section.t: where the sum and the products are computed in GF(2^8). The source symbols themselves are sent unchanged.

Short blocks. A block whose SSB_length is less than K uses only the first SSB_length rows of A. Its repair symbols equal those of a block of K source symbols whose symbols at ESIs SSB_length to K - 1 are all zero, because a zero symbol adds nothing to any sum. No zero symbol is sent or counted in SSB_length (Section 7.4).

Decoding. Every square submatrix of a Cauchy matrix is invertible ( Clause 6.2), so the code is maximum distance separable: a receiver that holds any SSB_length distinct symbols of a block, source and repair in any mix, recovers every source symbol of the block. Let M be the set of ESIs of the source symbols it lacks, and R a set of |M| RS_IDs of repair symbols that it holds. For each byte position u and each j in R:
section.artwork: sum over i in M of A_{i,j} * s_i[u] = r_j[u] + sum over i < SSB_length, i not in M, of A_{i,j} * s_i[u]
section.t: The square matrix of the entries A_{i,j} with i in M and j in R is a submatrix of A and is therefore invertible. The receiver inverts it once per block and applies the result at every byte position. Any decoding method that yields the same source symbols is acceptable.

The field is that of , but the generator matrix is not the Vandermonde-derived matrix of Section 8.2, and this document uses neither the FEC Payload IDs nor the source block partitioning of . Several systematic Reed-Solomon constructions over GF(2^8) are in use, and they produce different repair symbols from the same source symbols. Appendix C gives test vectors that tell this construction apart from the others.

section.name: Reed-Solomon Parameters
section.t: As for RaptorQ (Section 4.2), no decoder configuration is carried on the wire, and the code has no OTI to carry. When a track's catalog fec.algorithm is "reed-solomon", receivers MUST configure the decoder of each FEC block from the catalog fields (Section 5.1) and the block's Repair FEC Payload ID (Section 7.1), under the source symbol construction of the track's block profile (Sections 7.3 and 7.6.1), as follows:

ul.li: Symbol size: T = symbolSize. Every source and repair symbol is exactly T bytes. The RaptorQ rule that T is a multiple of 8 (Section 4.2) does not apply.
Rows: SSB_length, the block's source symbol count. The source symbol whose SS_ID is x is row (x - SS_Start) mod 2^32 of A, which is its ESI (Section 8.3).
Columns: the repair symbol whose RS_ID is j is column j of A. Its ESI, SSB_length + RS_ID (Section 7.2), still identifies it within its block, but the column depends on RS_ID alone.
Column count: RSB_length, the instance's total repair count P (Section 7.1).

section.t: This derivation is normative and complete: a receiver that has a track's catalog fec object requires no additional signaling to configure its decoder (Section 5.2). As under RaptorQ, its per-block inputs travel in the Repair FEC Payload ID of every repair packet of the block.

The catalog keeps every FEC instance under "reed-solomon" within the bound of Section 4.4: K + P is at most 255, where K is the instance's sourceSymbols and P its total repair count over all its repair layers (Section 6.3.4, rule 12). SSB_length + RSB_length is then at most 255 in every block. In addition to the checks of Section 7.4, a receiver MUST discard a repair packet of such a track whose SSB_length + RSB_length exceeds 255, or whose RS_ID is not less than RSB_length, leaving the state of every block unchanged. Neither packet is a symbol of a code that Section 4.4 defines. A repair packet whose RSB_length is less than O_i + P_i for a layer i that the receiver holds, of that layer's own track where i is above 0 or of a block to which the check of Section 6.3.9 applies, is handled by that section, which fails closed, and not by this rule; on any other packet this rule applies to it, one of a block generated before an append, carrying no symbol of layer i, or one of layer 0's track generated under a previous total (Section 6.3.9).

Repair layers (Section 6.3) carry disjoint ranges of columns: layer i carries columns O_i to O_i + P_i - 1 (Section 6.3.2). A column depends on its RS_ID alone, so a repair symbol is the same whichever layer carries it and whatever other layers exist, and symbols from any subset of layers combine in one decode. A keyframe overlay (Section 6.4) is a separate FEC instance, with its own rows, numbered from its overlay SS_IDs, its own columns and its own bound: K_overlay + P_overlay is at most 255, whatever the base instance uses.
For example, this catalog protects an mmtp track under "reed-solomon":

K + P is 32 + 8 = 40, within the bound. A full block uses rows 0 to 31 and columns 0 to 7 of A, and its repair packets carry SSB_length 32 and RSB_length 8. A short block of 20 source symbols uses rows 0 to 19 and the same columns, and its repair packets carry SSB_length 20. The repair symbol with RS_ID 3 is column 3 in both blocks, at ESI 35 in the first and ESI 23 in the second. The full block recovers once the receiver holds any 32 of its 40 symbols, and the short block once it holds any 20 of its 28. Rule 12 leaves room for repair layers (Section 6.3.9) of at most 215 more repair symbols in all, since 32 + 8 + 215 = 255, and Section 14.3 recommends far fewer.

section.name: Catalog Fields
section.t: The catalog (Section 5.2) is an MSF catalog , delivered on the track named catalog ( Section 5); for mmtp tracks it is extended by the documents of this suite as described in Section 12. This document adds one track-level field -- the fec object defined below -- and one packaging value (fec-repair, below). The FEC configuration is carried at the track level:
(Appendix B works this parameter set through in full. Section 7.6.7 shows a loc track under moq-object-v1, and Section 4.5 a track under "reed-solomon".)
Field definitions:
algorithm (string, REQUIRED if fec present): FEC scheme identifier.

ul.li: "none": No FEC
"raptorq": RaptorQ per RFC 6330 (OPTIONAL, Section 4.3)
"reed-solomon": Reed-Solomon over GF(2^8) per Section 4.4 (mandatory to implement, Section 4.3)

section.t: blockProfile (string, REQUIRED when algorithm is not "none"): The block profile of the track's FEC: the rules that fix how source symbols are formed from a source packet or a source object, how many source symbols a block holds, how a block and the source symbols in it are identified, and how those identifiers wrap. It applies to every FEC instance of the source track, its repair layers (Section 6.3) and any keyframe overlay (Section 6.4) included, and a repair track carries no blockProfile of its own (Section 6.3.4, rule 8). A publisher MUST NOT change a published track's blockProfile; a different profile is a different rendition. A fec object whose algorithm is "none" declares no FEC instance and need not carry blockProfile. This document defines two values, which Section 15.4 registers. Each admits only the source track packaging values named with it:

li.t: "iso-ssbg1-v1": the ISO/IEC 23008-1 Annex C profile of this document, all of whose rules a receiver applies together. It admits mmtp. A source symbol is the ssbg_mode1 framing of one FEC source packet (Section 7.3). A block holds SSB_length source symbols, with sourceSymbols as the upper bound on SSB_length (Section 7.4). SS_IDs advance by one per FEC source packet, blocks are consecutive, and a source symbol is placed in its block by range membership (Section 8.3). SS_ID arithmetic is modulo 2^32, and a block's repair objects are grouped under its 62-bit extended SS_Start (Section 7.5). An in-band AL-FEC message that describes such a track carries the coding byte 0x14 (Section 7.3).

"moq-object-v1": the object profile of this document (Section 7.6), all of whose rules a receiver applies together. It admits loc and cmaf. The Protected Object Unit of a source object spans s(o) consecutive source symbols (Section 7.6.1). A block holds whole units, SSB_length source symbols in all, with sourceSymbols as the upper bound on SSB_length (Section 7.6.2). SS_IDs advance by s(o) per source object, blocks are consecutive, and a source symbol is placed in its block by range membership (Section 8.3). SS_ID arithmetic and repair Group IDs are those of Section 7.5. A repair object carries no MMTP header (Section 7.6.3). The profile defines no in-band signaling and no keyframe overlay (Section 7.6.6).

section.t: A receiver MUST NOT apply FEC to a track whose blockProfile is absent, names a profile the receiver does not implement, or names a profile that does not admit the track's packaging. It treats FEC as unavailable for that track, as for an unimplemented algorithm (Section 4.3): it consumes the source track without FEC and does not subscribe to or join the track's repair tracks, and it MUST NOT fail the session, or FEC for any other track, on that account. There is no default profile, and a receiver MUST NOT infer one from the wire, whether from the fields of an in-band AL-FEC message, from the length of the source packets it receives, or from any other observation.

sourceSymbols (integer, REQUIRED): K, the largest number of source symbols an FEC block may hold. MUST be >= 1. It is an upper bound, not the size of each block: a block holds SSB_length source symbols, 1 <= SSB_length <= K (Section 7.4). Under iso-ssbg1-v1 it is the value an in-band AL-FEC message carries as maximum_k_for_repair_flow ( Clause C.6.3), which is likewise a maximum. K counts source symbols, not objects: under moq-object-v1 a source object contributes s(o) of them (Section 7.6.1). Under "reed-solomon", K plus the instance's total repair count is at most 255 (Section 6.3.4, rule 12).
repairSymbols (integer, REQUIRED): P value - repair symbols per FEC block. MUST be >= 1 when a repair track is published.

symbolSize (integer, REQUIRED): T value - bytes per symbol. T MUST be at least 1 under every block profile: a zero-length symbol carries nothing, and the symbol count of Section 7.6.1 divides by T. All symbols in a block have the same size; the byte layout of each source symbol is fixed by the track's blockProfile and is not otherwise carried in the catalog. Under "iso-ssbg1-v1" it is the ssbg_mode1 construction of Section 7.3, under which a source packet of up to T - 2 bytes is protected; under it T MUST be at least 14: a shorter symbol carries no protected packet of the 12-octet MMTP packet header ( Section 3.1). Under "moq-object-v1" it is the construction of Section 7.6.1, under which an object whose Protected Object Unit is at most K x T bytes long is protected. For "raptorq", T is a multiple of 8, the fixed Symbol Alignment of the derived OTI (Section 4.2), so the least T is 8 under "moq-object-v1" and 16 under "iso-ssbg1-v1". For "reed-solomon", no such alignment applies (Section 4.5).

interleaveDepthMs (integer, OPTIONAL): When present, its value MUST be a non-negative integer. A value greater than zero is the complete FEC source/repair packet send span in milliseconds. It is the catalog form of protection_window_time in Sections 11.2 and C.6.3: the actual elapsed time from sending the first source or repair packet of a block to sending the last source or repair packet of that block MUST NOT exceed this value. For a positive value it is a duration, never a count of frames, groups, samples, or symbols, and never a per-symbol interval.

This field does not select FEC block boundaries, the number of source symbols in a block, the number of blocks in a MoQ Group, or the number of groups a block spans. Those are determined by the consecutive source SS_ID values and the (SS_Start, SSB_length) carried by the block's repair packets (Sections 7.4 and 8.3). A block MAY contain part of a Group, one Group, or several Groups, and a Group MAY contain more than one block.
Thus interleaveDepthMs and groupDurationMs are not inputs to block assignment; Section 8.3 specifies the source-symbol range and repair packet fields that assign a source symbol to a block.

When present with a value greater than zero, a publisher chooses this value to cover the actual source/repair send span of every block. An absent field supplies no catalog-signaled span. A value of zero has the ISO meaning of using protection_window_size instead of a time window Clause C.6.3 under iso-ssbg1-v1; this catalog profile carries no packet-count window. Under moq-object-v1, which has no in-band signaling (Section 5.2), a value of zero is equivalent to an absent field. A catalog-only receiver therefore MUST NOT treat zero as a zero-duration span or use it to derive a block count, and has no elapsed-time FEC deadline from this field. If an applicable ISO packet-count window is accepted in-band, it governs separate count-based processing; it does not supply a millisecond deadline, and the receiver MUST NOT assume a media cadence to convert it. Without an elapsed-time deadline, open-block state is bounded only by the local policy of Section 9, and on a multicast or AMT leg the receiver performs no block classification or unicast repair (Section 11.4) and keeps its repair-layer selection fixed (Section 6.3.6).

reorderToleranceMs (number, OPTIONAL): A receiver-local allowance for packet reordering, network jitter, and local processing variance, in milliseconds. When present, the value MUST be finite and MUST be greater than or equal to zero; fractional values are permitted. An explicit value of zero means that no additional allowance is required. An omitted field means that the publisher did not signal an allowance; receivers MUST preserve that distinction from an explicit zero.

For a receiver that uses a positive interleaveDepthMs, the FEC block deadline is the receiver-local timestamp of the first accepted packet plus the complete block span. When reorderToleranceMs is present, its catalog allowance is then added:
section.artwork: base_deadline = firstAcceptedAtMs + interleaveDepthMs deadline = base_deadline + reorderToleranceMs // when present
section.t: The catalog allowance is added exactly once when present. Its absence is not equivalent to an explicitly signaled zero; a receiver that applies an explicit local policy MUST keep that policy separate from the catalog value. When interleaveDepthMs is absent or zero, this formula supplies no elapsed-time FEC deadline; an applicable ISO packet-count window, if accepted in-band, remains separate count-based processing and is not converted to milliseconds. A receiver whose FEC deadline API requires a signaled allowance MUST reject or disable FEC for a track that omits reorderToleranceMs.
repairTrack (string, REQUIRED): The Track Name of the layer-0 repair track, which is in the source track's Track Namespace (Section 6.1).

Repair tracks themselves are identified in the catalog by the packaging value "fec-repair": a track with "packaging": "fec-repair" carries repair objects (Section 7) for the source track whose fec.repairTrack field names it, and carries no directly renderable media. The value extends the allowed packaging values of Section 5.2.4 in the same manner as the cmaf value of ; see Section 15.3. Receivers that do not implement this specification do not recognize the value and ignore such tracks.

enhancementRepair: Not defined. Repair layers and keyframe overlays are declared on their own repair-track entries (Section 5.1.1), and a catalog carrying this member is rejected under the exceptions there.

section.name: Repair Track Fields
section.t: A track with "packaging": "fec-repair" describes its own role. It carries the flat MSF track fields plus the fields below. Layer 0 is identified by the source's fec.repairTrack; its entry MAY also carry depends, "repairLayer": 0 and repairSymbols, which MUST agree with the source's corresponding field when present (Section 6.3.4, rules 2 and 11).

depends (array of strings, REQUIRED except on layer 0): The name of the source track this track repairs. The array MUST contain exactly one name, and that name MUST identify a track in the same catalog that carries an fec object whose blockProfile admits the track's packaging (Section 5.1).
repairLayer (integer, REQUIRED on enhancement layers, OPTIONAL on layer 0, MUST NOT appear on an overlay): The layer index (Section 6.3).

repairSymbols (integer, REQUIRED except on layer 0; MUST be >= 1): The repair symbols per block that this track carries, P_i. For layer 0 the source track's fec.repairSymbols is the authoritative P_0 (Section 6.3.4, rule 11).

priority (integer, OPTIONAL): The Publisher Priority ( Section 5.1.1) of this track's objects, in the range 192 to 255 (Section 10). A publisher that declares it MUST give every object of the track this Publisher Priority, for example through the track's DEFAULT_PUBLISHER_PRIORITY Track Property ( Section 10.4). Subscriber priority is applied before publisher priority ( Section 5.1.2), so a subscriber SHOULD NOT subscribe to the track with a SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY numerically lower than that of its subscription to the source track. It MAY use this value as that SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY.

scope (string, OPTIONAL): When present, MUST be "keyframe", and declares this track to be the source track's keyframe overlay (Section 6.4). It is one of the unknown-key exceptions below. An overlay is defined only for a source track under iso-ssbg1-v1 (Section 6.3.4, rule 10).
sourceSymbols (integer, REQUIRED on an overlay, MUST NOT appear otherwise; MUST be >= 1): The overlay instance's own K, the upper bound on the SSB_length of its blocks (Section 7.4).

Track names carry no meaning in any of this. A receiver MUST resolve every relationship from fec.repairTrack, depends, repairLayer and scope, and MUST NOT infer one by parsing a track name or a name suffix.

A receiver MUST ignore a track-level or fec object key that it does not recognize, and MUST NOT treat its presence as an error, so that this suite can add fields without a flag day. Exactly three keys defined by this document are exceptions, because ignoring any of them would change how the receiver must interpret the packets it receives:

ul.li: fec.enhancementRepair: a receiver MUST reject a catalog carrying it.
scope: a receiver that does not implement overlays MUST fail closed on a catalog carrying it (Section 6.4).
fec.blockProfile: a receiver MUST NOT apply FEC to a track whose blockProfile names a profile it does not implement (Section 5.1).

section.name: Worked Catalog
section.t: Three repair layers and one keyframe overlay on one mmtp source track:
A receiver derives the following from that catalog, the ESI column for a full block; none of it is carried on the wire:

The RS_ID ranges are fixed by the catalog. The ESI ranges are those of a full block: a repair symbol's ESI is the block's SSB_length plus its RS_ID (Section 7.2), so in a short block every ESI range moves down by 64 - SSB_length while the RS_ID ranges do not move.

The total repair count is 8 + 16 + 32 = 56, so RSB_length is 56 on every repair packet of layers 0, 1 and 2 (Section 7.1). The overlay is a separate FEC instance and is not in that table: its own K is 256, its own P is 32, its RS_ID range is 0 to 31, its ESI range in a full overlay block is 256 to 287, and its packets carry RSB_length 32.
This catalog uses raptorq. Under reed-solomon its base instance would be valid, since 64 + 56 = 120 is at most 255, but its overlay would not, since 256 + 32 = 288 exceeds 255 (Section 6.4.1).
The layer arithmetic is the same under moq-object-v1, which defines no overlay.

section.name: Signaling Model
section.t: The catalog fec object (Section 5.1) is the authoritative FEC signaling for MoQ receivers, that is for every receiver that obtains the track's catalog entry. Such a receiver has everything needed to discover and subscribe to the repair track (Section 6) and to configure its decoder from the derived parameters (Sections 4.2 and 4.5); no in-session signaling is required.

A packaging profile MAY also define in-band FEC signaling carried with the media, which serves a receiver that consumes a flow without the catalog. For the mmtp packaging this is the AL-FEC message of Clause C.6 ( Sections 8 and 8.3). The loc and cmaf packagings define none, so for a track under moq-object-v1 the catalog is the only FEC signaling. In-band FEC signaling MUST NOT signal FEC parameters that contradict the track's catalog fec object. Where the two disagree the catalog governs for a MoQ receiver, and a MoQ receiver MUST NOT require in-band signaling in order to configure its decoder.

The catalog's authority holds uniformly across a MoQ receiver's delivery paths, its multicast and AMT legs included. MoQ control messages cannot reach multicast or sessionless receivers at all (Section 11), so no control-message mechanism could serve as the common signaling path; the catalog can, because it is delivered as track data or out of band.

section.name: FEC Source Info Object Property
section.t: A publisher that carries FEC source symbols as MoQ objects MUST tag each object that carries one or more source symbols with a FEC Source Info Object Property, whose type is the odd value 0x11 (Section 15.1). Under moq-object-v1 that is every source object (Section 7.6.2).

0x11 is the value this document requests, and the registration policy for the range it lies in is not reachable by an individual draft (Section 15.1). Until that request is resolved, 0x11 is to be read as provisional. If it is not obtainable, Section 15.1 names an odd value in the range 0x80 to 0x37FF as the fallback. That value can take a 2-byte Delta Type ( Section 8.3), so adopting it can change the length of an object's Properties on the wire and not only the constant in this paragraph.

calls these Object Properties; drafts before draft-17 called them object extension headers, and the two terms name the same wire construct. It encodes a Property as a key-value pair whose type parity selects the value encoding: an even type carries a single variable-length integer, an odd type carries a length-prefixed sequence of bytes. FEC Source Info is byte-valued, so its type is odd, and a receiver or relay that knows nothing of this document still steps over the Property correctly by its length prefix. A relay that does not implement this document forwards the Property unmodified and caches it with the object, as Section 8.4 requires of any Property that a relay does not support.

Deployed implementations have used the even value 0x10 for this purpose. That value is not available: already lists 0x10 as the TIMESTAMP Object Property of draft-ietf-moq-loc, in the same Property Type space and at the same Object scope. A 0x10-tagged FEC object is therefore not merely unparseable under the parity rule; it is a semantic collision with an unrelated Property. A receiver that implements TIMESTAMP parses the FEC Source Info value as a variable-length integer, yields a garbage timestamp, and then reads the next Property type out of the middle of the FEC Source Info bytes. The key-value sequence may be desynchronized from that point on. Depending on the bytes, the parse ends in a session closure ( Section 8.3), in a malformed track ( Sections 10.7 and 12.1), or in silently wrong Property values. A Delta Type read out of the FEC Source Info bytes that overflows 2^64-1, or a Length that exceeds 2^16-1, is a PROTOCOL_VIOLATION; a type that is understood but whose value does not match its serialization is a KEY_VALUE_FORMATTING_ERROR. This is why implementations that use 0x10 must special-case the type ahead of the parity rule to interoperate at all. An implementation of this document MUST NOT send 0x10. The defence is necessarily publisher-side: a receiver cannot detect a 0x10-tagged FEC object as such, because by construction it is indistinguishable from a well-formed TIMESTAMP. A receiver cannot reject a 0x10 Property and carry on either, because by the time it has mis-parsed the value the sequence may already be desynchronized.
The Property value is:

SS_ID is an unsigned integer in network byte order. Under iso-ssbg1-v1 it is the sequence number of the source symbol the object carries (Section 2), the same value and the same definition that the Source FEC Payload ID trailer of a FEC source packet carries on the MMTP path (Section 8.5). This Property is that trailer's MoQ-layer carrier: one identifier, one definition, whichever path the symbol travels. Under moq-object-v1 it is the SS_ID of the first of the s(o) source symbols that the object's Protected Object Unit occupies (Section 7.6.2), and the Property is the only carrier of that value: the profile has no trailer.

Where the packaging also delivers the trailer, both carry the same value and a publisher MUST make them identical. On the mmtp packaging of that is every source object, because the object payload is the whole FEC source packet, trailer included. The Property is wanted there as well: it places the symbol at the MoQ layer, reachable by a relay and by a receiver that does not parse MMTP, whereas the trailer is the field the FEC encoder emitted and the one Section 8.3 locates the symbol by. Where the two disagree the trailer prevails (Section 8.5). A packet the decoder recovers carries neither (Section 7.3): the Property is not recovered with the object, and the trailer is appended after FEC encoding, so a receiver that recovers a packet determines its SS_ID from the block coordinate that recovered it, within that FEC instance's SS_ID space (Section 6.4.1); an overlay coordinate does not yield a base SS_ID (Section 7.3). Under moq-object-v1 a Property carried inside Immutable Properties is part of the Protected Object Unit and is recovered with the object, but a receiver still takes a recovered object's SS_ID from the block coordinate at which it found the unit, and checks the Property against it (Section 7.6.4).

Where a keyframe overlay applies (Section 6.4), an object carrying a Random Access Point fragment is a source symbol of two FEC instances, whose SS_ID spaces are disjoint (Section 6.4.1), so "the source symbol the object carries" names two SS_IDs rather than one. This Property carries the base instance's SS_ID -- the value the Source FEC Payload ID trailer carries on the MMTP path (Section 8.5.1) -- and a publisher MUST NOT place an overlay SS_ID in it. No second Property conveys the overlay SS_ID: it travels in the 0x8B01 MMTP header extension, which lies inside the MMTP packet header and is therefore part of the protected packet of both instances (Section 8.5.1), so it rides inside the object's payload on this path as on any other. A receiver takes an overlay SS_ID from that extension and from nothing else, and in particular MUST NOT infer one from this Property (Section 8.5.1).

A receiver places the symbol in a block by SS_ID (Section 8.3) and learns the block's extent from the (SS_Start, SSB_length) of a repair object (Section 7.1), exactly as on the MMTP path. The Property carries no block coordinate, and a receiver MUST NOT infer one from it: the constraints of Section 7.4 on delimiting a block apply unchanged to a MoQ receiver, so it MUST NOT infer a block boundary, or SSB_length, from a gap in SS_IDs, from a group or MPU boundary -- which for a MoQ receiver includes a Group boundary -- from elapsed time, or from sourceSymbols. Until it has accepted a repair object of the block it holds the symbol without placing it, as Section 8.3 describes.

FEC Source Info is single-valued. An object carries at most one FEC Source Info Property, counting its mutable Properties and its Immutable Properties together ( Section 10.7). A receiver treats an object that carries more than one as an object that carries none (below).

An object that carries a source symbol but no FEC Source Info Property violates the publisher requirement that opens this section. A receiver that does not parse the FEC source packet has no SS_ID for it -- at the MoQ layer the Property is the only carrier -- so it MUST NOT feed such an object to the base decoder and MUST NOT count it in K or in any base block, and MAY still deliver it as media. Where the packaging delivers the trailer, a receiver that parses the packet MAY take the SS_ID from there instead (Section 8.3). An overlay SS_ID is unaffected either way: it travels in the 0x8B01 MMTP header extension (Section 8.5.1), which this Property does not carry, and Section 8.5.1 alone governs when the overlay decoder may be fed.

The value is exactly 4 bytes. A value of any other length does not match the serialization defined for this type, so a receiver that implements this document MUST close the session with KEY_VALUE_FORMATTING_ERROR, as requires of any Property whose type is understood and whose value does not match.

SS_ID is a fixed 32-bit field rather than a variable-length integer for two reasons. First, does not require its variable-length integers to be encoded in the minimum number of bytes, so one numeric value has several valid encodings that differ in length; a varint field inside the Property value would therefore vary the Property's own length without varying its meaning. Second, the encoding is a property of the session: replaced it at draft-17 (transport issue 1016) with a leading-1-bits scheme that is not the QUIC variable-length integer encoding of earlier drafts and does not decode the same bytes to the same values, so a varint field following the session encoding would decode differently on two drafts. A fixed width removes both. A publisher and a receiver that negotiated different session versions, and a relay that re-encodes between them, decode this field identically.

This Property carries no object length. A receiver that recovers an object by FEC decoding does not recover its mutable Properties, and under iso-ssbg1-v1 it recovers no Properties at all, so a length carried here could be absent in exactly the case a recovered length is wanted. The recoverable length is inside the source symbols themselves, and is recovered with them: the Length field of Section 7.3, or the Immutable Properties Length and Payload Length of the Protected Object Unit (Section 7.6.1). Under both source symbol constructions the padding that completes a symbol is applied by the encoder and decoder and is not transmitted, so there is no transmitted padding for a receiver to strip.

section.name: Track Naming
section.t: A repair track MUST be in the Track Namespace of the source track it repairs. The fec.repairTrack and depends fields carry only a Track Name ( Section 2.4.1), and a receiver resolves each in that namespace, as Section 5.2.14 does for depends.
By convention, the layer-0 repair track's Track Name is the source track's Track Name followed by the seven bytes "/repair":

The name is a convention and not a resolution mechanism: a receiver resolves every repair track from fec.repairTrack, depends, repairLayer and scope (Section 5.1.1), so the name serves only human readers, in logs and configuration. Enhancement layers (Section 6.3) and a keyframe overlay (Section 6.4) have no conventional name. A receiver MUST NOT infer that a track is a repair track, which source it repairs, or which layer it is, by parsing a track name or a name suffix, and a publisher MUST NOT rely on a receiver doing so. Names such as "video/repair/1" appear in the examples of this document for readability only.

section.name: Subscription Model
section.t: Subscribers SHOULD subscribe to the source track first, then subscribe to the repair track if:

ol.li: The track's catalog entry signals FEC (a fec object naming a repairTrack, Section 5.1), AND
The subscriber desires FEC protection

section.t: Repair-track subscription is selective and per-need: a subscriber chooses whether to consume repair data based on its own path conditions, and MAY start or stop its repair-track subscription at any time during the session -- for example, subscribing only after observing loss, or not subscribing at all on a reliable path.

Publishers and relays MUST NOT require subscription to repair tracks and MUST NOT condition delivery of a source track on a repair-track subscription. Repair tracks are optional; subscribers MAY choose to rely solely on QUIC retransmission or to accept unrecovered loss.

section.name: Layered Repair Tracks
section.t: A source track MAY be protected by more than one repair track. Each such track is a repair layer: an independently subscribable set of repair symbols for the same source blocks. Layer 0 is the repair track named by repairTrack, carrying the source's repairSymbols symbols per block. Layers 1..n are the tracks that name this source in depends and carry a repairLayer (Section 5.1.1), one track per layer index.

Under iso-ssbg1-v1, layered repair is an extension of that an ISO AL-FEC message cannot express: each FEC source flow has one FEC encoded flow, whose one-stage coding structure carries a single repair_flow_id ( Clause C.6.3), so only layer 0 maps to an ISO repair flow. An in-band AL-FEC message names layer 0 and no other layer ( Section 8.3). A repair layer is also unrelated to the layers of ISO layer-aware FEC (LA-FEC, Clause C.2.3).

Layering separates the two costs of FEC: the repair count P buys tolerance to random loss at a cost in bandwidth, and the interleave window buys tolerance to burst loss at a cost in recovery latency (Section 9). Layers let a receiver on a lossier path add repair without changing the source encoding. A source track names only layer 0; each further layer declares itself on its own tracks entry, so the layer set is validated as a whole (Section 6.3.4) and changed only as Section 6.3.9 allows. An entity that republishes a subset of a catalog MUST NOT list a fec-repair track whose source track it omits (Section 6.3.4, rule 9).

section.name: Shared Block Geometry
section.t: All repair layers of a source track share its block geometry (algorithm, blockProfile, sourceSymbols, symbolSize, interleaveDepthMs, reorderToleranceMs) and differ only in repairSymbols. A repair layer MUST NOT carry a geometry field; rule 8 of Section 6.3.4 lists them, and a receiver rejects a catalog that violates it. Because each source packet or source object carries one base SS_ID (Sections 5.3 and 8.5), a different K or interleave window needs a separate rendition; the keyframe overlay (Section 6.4) is a separate FEC instance, not a layer.

section.name: Repair Symbol Identity Across Layers
section.t: Let P_i be the repairSymbols of layer i and O_i its RS_ID offset, defined below (O_0 = 0). P_0 is the source track's fec.repairSymbols (Section 6.3.4, rule 11), and P_i for i >= 1 the layer track's own repairSymbols. Layer i carries, for every source block, the repair symbols with RS_ID in [O_i, O_i + P_i). The Encoding Symbol ID follows the single-layer rule of Section 7.2:
section.artwork: O_i = sum(P_j for j < i) RS_ID = O_i + j, for the j-th symbol of layer i ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID
section.t: where SSB_length is the block's source symbol count (Section 7.1).

The total repair count of the block is the sum of P_i over all published layers. RSB_length on every repair packet of every layer carries this total (Section 7.1), not the layer's own P_i. That is what makes the RS_ID to ESI mapping independent of which layers a given receiver joined: a receiver holding a non-prefix subset computes the same coordinate for a symbol as a receiver holding everything, and the RS_ID < RSB_length bound holds for a symbol from any layer.

Under either code of this document, a repair symbol is fixed by its block and its RS_ID alone, whichever layer carries it, and any set of distinct encoding symbols of a block decodes together (; Section 4.4). Symbols received from any subset of layers, over any mix of paths, therefore combine in one decode. Subsets need not be prefixes: in the worked catalog of Section 5.1.2 a receiver holding layers 0 and 2 holds, for a full block, ESIs 64 to 71 and 88 to 119, which are distinct encoding symbols of one code, and it decodes as soon as it holds enough distinct symbols in total.

A receiver that has subscribed a set of layers recovers a block whenever the number of lost symbols, source and repair together, does not exceed C - e, where C is the total P over the layers it holds and e is the decoding overhead of the track's algorithm: 0 under reed-solomon, which is maximum distance separable (Section 4.4), and under raptorq a small number of symbols (roughly 1e-2, 1e-4, and 1e-6 residual failure at 0, 1, and 2 symbols of overhead per ). This loss tolerance is derived from K and the layer counts; it MUST NOT be signaled as a separate catalog field.
Receivers MUST take layer membership and per-layer counts from the catalog. RSB_length carries the total and says nothing about which layers a receiver holds.

On layer i, the block's repair objects form the MoQ group whose Group ID is the block's extended SS_Start (Section 7.5), and that group carries P_i objects (Section 7); object j of that group carries the repair symbol with RS_ID = O_i + j.

section.name: Algorithms That Admit Layers
section.t: Repair layers and the overlay are defined only for raptorq and reed-solomon: a publisher MUST NOT signal either under any other algorithm, and a receiver rejects such a catalog (Section 6.3.4, rule 7).

Layering needs a code whose repair symbols are identified by ESI alone and whose repair symbol for a given ESI does not depend on how many repair symbols the block generates in total. Only then do repair symbols from disjoint ESI ranges on separate tracks remain symbols of one code, and only then can a receiver add a layer without the publisher re-encoding. RaptorQ has this property by construction, through its open Encoding Symbol ID space (). The property is not particular to fountain codes. A systematic Reed-Solomon code whose generator matrix is Vandermonde-derived ( Section 8.2.1) or Cauchy-derived has it too, provided the field element that defines each repair column is fixed by the symbol's index in the code and never by P. fixes it as alpha^j for the Encoding Symbol ID j, so a repair column is fixed by SSB_length and RS_ID together, through ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID. The Cauchy construction of Section 4.4 fixes y_j as alpha^j for RS_ID j, so a repair column is fixed by RS_ID alone. Each repair symbol is then one fixed column of that matrix, independent of the code length n = K + totalP, and the field size is the only bound: K + totalP is at most 2^m - 1 over GF(2^m) for the construction, and at most 2^m for a Cauchy construction in general. The construction of Section 4.4, whose x_i and y_j are nonzero powers of alpha, allows 2^m - 1, that is 255. A Reed-Solomon code in generator-polynomial form lacks the property: its parity is the remainder modulo a polynomial of degree n - K, so its symbols for one P are not valid for another.

An algorithm admits repair layers and the overlay only if its specification (a) establishes this property for the construction it specifies, including that each repair column's field element is fixed by the symbol's index in the code alone, (b) states how each layer's RS_ID range maps to that code's symbol index (for , the Encoding Symbol ID, whose Max-Number-of-Encoding-Symbols then covers K + totalP over all layers), (c) bounds K + totalP by that construction's limit, alongside rules 4 and 5 of Section 6.3.4, and (d) updates rule 7 of Section 6.3.4, since a receiver of this document otherwise rejects such a catalog. Rule 6 is particular to RaptorQ.

The reed-solomon code of Section 4.4 meets all four conditions: (a) column j of A depends on RS_ID j alone, through y_j = alpha^j, and not on P or on SSB_length; (b) layer i carries columns O_i to O_i + P_i - 1 (Section 4.5); (c) rule 12 of Section 6.3.4 bounds K + totalP by 255 for each FEC instance; and (d) rule 7 admits it. A specification of another algorithm can admit repair layers and the overlay on the same terms.

section.name: Catalog Rules and Fail-Closed Validation
section.t: A receiver MUST validate all of the following for a source track before starting FEC for it. On any violation the receiver MUST fail closed: it MUST report the offending catalog path and MUST NOT start FEC for that source track. A receiver MUST NOT repair the catalog by ignoring the offending track, because every rule below distinguishes a layer set that decodes from one that silently mis-maps symbols.

ol.li: depends names exactly one track in the same catalog, which carries an fec object whose blockProfile admits that track's packaging (Section 5.1).
The repairLayer values for one source track are contiguous from 1 to n, with no gaps and no duplicates. Layer 0 is the track named by the source's fec.repairTrack.

priority, where declared, is in the range 192 to 255 inclusive, and is monotonic non-decreasing with layer index. Layer 0's priority MAY be declared on its own track; when absent it is 240, and the publisher MUST give the layer-0 track's objects Publisher Priority 240.
For each FEC instance, the total of repairSymbols across all its layers is at most 2^24 - 1, the range of RSB_length.
For each FEC instance, K + totalP - 1 is at most 2^24 - 1, which bounds the largest ESI the instance can produce.

When fec.algorithm is raptorq, K is at most 56403 for each FEC instance. extends a source block of K source symbols to K' symbols, the smallest value at least K in its Table 2 ( Section 5.3.1), and 56403 is the largest such value, K'_max ( Section 5.1.2), so a RaptorQ source block holds at most 56403 source symbols.
Repair layers and any overlay appear only when fec.algorithm is raptorq or reed-solomon (Section 6.3.3 above).

A track whose packaging is fec-repair carries no geometry field, whether as a flat field or inside an fec object of its own: algorithm, blockProfile, mmtpMode, timescale, any groupDuration field, symbolSize, interleaveDepthMs, reorderToleranceMs, and sourceSymbols except on an overlay (Section 6.4).

No orphan repair track: every track whose packaging is fec-repair is reachable from a source track, either by being named in that source's fec.repairTrack or by naming that source in depends. This rule binds once the catalog declares any FEC source, that is any track whose fec.algorithm is not none; a catalog that declares no FEC source at all MAY carry an unreferenced fec-repair track that nothing joins. This rule is the one exception to the per-source remedy of the preamble above: an orphan track is by definition associated with no source track, so there is no source track to stop. The receiver MUST refuse to join the orphan track and MUST report its catalog path, and MUST NOT stop FEC for any source track on account of it.

A source track has at most one track with "scope": "keyframe" (Section 6.4), and none when its fec.blockProfile is moq-object-v1 (Section 7.6.6). A track with "scope": "keyframe" carries no repairLayer.

The layer-0 repair track's repairSymbols, where declared, equals the source track's fec.repairSymbols. The source field is the single authoritative value of P_0; the layer-0 track MAY restate it and MUST restate it identically. A receiver MUST reject a catalog declaring both with different values, and MUST NOT resolve the conflict by preferring either field, because the two readings disagree about O_1, about the block total, and therefore about the RSB_length that every layer's packets carry (Section 6.3.2). This rule is why rules 4, 5 and 12 have a single well defined totalP to bound.

When fec.algorithm is reed-solomon, K + totalP is at most 255 for each FEC instance: for the base instance, fec.sourceSymbols plus the repairSymbols of all its layers, and for an overlay, its own sourceSymbols plus its own repairSymbols (Sections 4.5 and 6.4.1). Every entry of A that a block of the instance uses is then defined (Section 4.4).

The fec object meets the range rules of Section 5.1: sourceSymbols is at least 1, repairSymbols is at least 1 when a repair track is published, symbolSize is at least 1 and, under iso-ssbg1-v1, at least 14, and symbolSize is a multiple of 8 when fec.algorithm is raptorq; and each repair track meets those of Section 5.1.1: its repairSymbols, where declared, is at least 1, and an overlay's sourceSymbols is at least 1. A symbol shorter than 14 octets carries no protected MMTP packet (Section 7.3), a RaptorQ symbol size off the Symbol Alignment fits no derived OTI (Section 4.2), and a block of no source or no repair symbols recovers nothing, in the base instance or in an overlay (Section 6.4.1), so a receiver that started FEC on such a catalog would join repair tracks whose symbols recover no packet.

section.t: Section 6.3.9 adds one check that can only be made on received repair packets.

The following are the fail-closed cases this section introduces, written against the worked catalog of Section 5.1.2 (K = 64, P_0 = 8, P_1 = 16, P_2 = 32) so that each defect is one edit away from a valid catalog. Each row violates the rule shown, and none of them is detectable from the wire.

tr.th: Why the wire cannot catch it

tr.td: video/repair declares repairSymbols 16 while the source declares fec.repairSymbols 8

Both readings are self-consistent: one derives O_1 = 8 and total 56, the other O_1 = 16 and total 64. A repair symbol is identified by ESI alone, so a receiver that resolved P_0 the other way decodes with a shifted mapping and reports a corrupt block, not a catalog error.
Both claim RS_ID 8 to 23. Symbols from the two tracks are distinct on the wire but collide in ESI, so a decode fed from both sees duplicate encoding symbols and stalls short of K.
video/repair/2 is present but no track declares layer 1
O_2 is a function of P_1, which is absent, so the receiver has no offset for layer 2 at all.
The overlay is a second FEC instance over its own K (Section 6.4). Admitting it as a layer would fold its RS_ID space into O_i and place its symbols in the base instance's ESI range.
A second track for video declares "scope": "keyframe"
A RAP packet carries one overlay SS_ID, in its one header extension (Section 8.5.1), so a second overlay has no SS_ID on the wire.
video/repair/1 carries symbolSize or its own fec object
A repair track carrying its own geometry would name itself as layer 0 and bypass rule 9's reachability check.

section.t: A receiver MAY report several violations at once.

section.name: Receiver Selection
section.t: The per-need model of Section 6.2 applies to each layer independently. On a lossy path a receiver SHOULD subscribe layer 0 first. When a block fails recovery with the receiver's current layer set and a higher layer exists, the receiver SHOULD subscribe the next layer; it MAY instead request only the failed block's repair objects from that layer, a request bounded to the block's repair group (Section 7.5), when the block is still inside its recovery budget (Section 9). On a multicast or AMT leg, Section 11.4 governs such per-block requests: which blocks get one, when, with what budget and priority, and what happens when one fails. A receiver MAY unsubscribe a layer after a receiver-chosen number of consecutive blocks whose loss stayed within the tolerance of the remaining layers. Hysteresis is counted in blocks, the protocol's unit, not by a fixed timer (Section 6.3.6).

section.name: Repair-Only Multicast Endpoints
section.t: Multicast endpoints carry only mmtp tracks and their repair tracks ( Section 4.1), so this subsection concerns tracks under iso-ssbg1-v1.

On a multicast endpoint the receiver cannot choose tracks; the operator of the endpoint chooses which tracks that path carries. Each repair layer carried on an endpoint is listed with its own packetId ( Section 4.1), exactly as a source track is, and a receiver MUST route every such packetId to the decoder of the source track that layer depends on. Because every endpoint carries the same source packets under the same block partition (Section 6.3.1), a receiver that moves between endpoints, or that is side-fed over MoQ unicast, mixes symbols from all of them in one decode. Layers not carried on any endpoint the receiver holds remain reachable over MoQ unicast (Section 6.2) for receivers that have a return path.

An operator MAY carry the source track and its layers together on one endpoint, or MAY place layers on endpoints of their own. An endpoint whose track list contains only fec-repair tracks is a repair-only endpoint:

The first endpoint suits a regional path with low random loss. The second is repair-only: a receiver on a lossy path holds both, and receives source packets once while adding layers 1 and 2 to the same decode.

A repair-only endpoint is never a media tier. A receiver MUST NOT treat one as a rendition or quality choice, and endpoint or ladder selection MUST exclude it on every path by which a receiver picks what to render. A repair-only endpoint's bandwidth ( Section 4.1) is the cost of adding repair to a stream the receiver has already selected, not the cost of an alternative rendition, and MUST NOT be compared against a media endpoint's bandwidth when choosing one.

A receiver joins a repair-only endpoint on measured loss: the rate at which its FEC blocks fail to recover, and the margin by which recovering blocks consume the repair symbols available to it. A receiver MUST NOT use goodput, throughput, or estimated available bandwidth to decide whether to add or drop a repair layer.

Layer changes are make-before-break. A receiver MUST join the additional layer's endpoint and begin receiving from it before leaving any endpoint it currently holds, so that no source block is left with less coverage than the receiver already had. A layer whose endpoint the receiver has left is carried on no endpoint it holds, reachable over MoQ unicast as above; under the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2 a receiver holds an endpoint while joined to its group, reading its manifest track or receiving the broadcast that carries the flow (its Section 7.2.9), and a consumer is protected under that endpoint's flow only while the receiver holds it (step 2 of Section 7.2.7).

Hysteresis MUST derive from the FEC block span, that is from interleaveDepthMs together with reorderToleranceMs, and MUST NOT come from a fixed timer or a fixed symbol count. A receiver MUST observe at least one full block span at the new layer set before making a further layer change.

That loss measure and this hysteresis both need a block deadline, which exists only for a positive interleaveDepthMs (Section 9). On a multicast or AMT leg, a receiver of a track whose catalog omits that field or sets it to zero MUST NOT add or drop a repair layer of the track on block-recovery evidence, and keeps its repair-layer selection for the track fixed.

section.name: Interaction with the Interleave Window
section.t: Layers never change interleaveDepthMs, the stream's single recovery-latency lever (Section 9). A shallow window recovers bursts only by per-block unicast repair (Sections 6.3.5 and 11.4.2), at about one round trip; a deep window recovers them in band at that window's latency. Serving both requires two renditions (Section 6.3.1).

section.name: Compatibility
section.t: A source track with a single repair track is the one-layer case (O_0 = 0, RSB_length = repairSymbols). A receiver that subscribes only layer 0 decodes correctly whatever other layers exist: layer 0 alone is a valid layer set, and it uses RSB_length only as a bound: RS_ID < RSB_length, and under reed-solomon also SSB_length + RSB_length <= 255 (Section 4.5). The keyframe overlay is the exception: a receiver has to recognize its declaration, because its repair packets belong to another FEC instance (Section 6.4.3).

section.name: Changing the Layer Set Within a Session
section.t: Publishing a layer is adding one tracks entry and withdrawing it is removing one, but the two directions are not symmetric, because O_i is a function of every lower layer's P (Section 6.3.2). A change to the set can therefore move the coordinates of a layer a receiver has already joined. This subsection states which changes are defined.

Layer sets are append-only. A publisher MAY append a layer at the next index above the highest published one; under reed-solomon the new total MUST keep the instance within rule 12 of Section 6.3.4. It MUST NOT withdraw a published layer, at any index, for the lifetime of the source encoding. An append changes O_i for no layer already published, because no published layer's set of lower layers changes. It does raise the total, so RSB_length on the wire rises, which is benign for the reason Section 6.3.8 gives: a receiver uses the total only as a bound, RS_ID < RSB_length and under reed-solomon also SSB_length + RSB_length <= 255, so a receiver holding a catalog from before an append reads a smaller bound that excludes only symbols of layers it has not joined. The other order needs care: a block's RSB_length is the total in force when its repair symbols were generated (Section 7.1), so the repair packets of a block generated under the previous total carry that total, which is O_n for the appended layer n and below O_n + P_n, and a receiver that joins layer n can take such a packet after the catalog that lists the layer: the packets of a block are sent over the span of Section 5.1 (interleaveDepthMs), a relay delivers from its cache, and a unicast repair (Section 11.4) returns the repair objects of an older block. The check below therefore applies, for a held layer above 0, to a repair packet of that layer's own track, which carries a symbol generated under a total at or above its O_i + P_i whatever block it belongs to, and, for every held layer, to a block at or after, in the serial order of their SS_Start (Section 7.5), the order blocks are generated in, one of which the receiver has received a repair packet carrying at least that layer's O_i + P_i; for a layer above 0, a block before it whose packets of other layers carry less was generated before the append, carries no symbol of the layer, and those packets are the symbols of the layers the receiver holds below it, under the coordinates of Section 6.3.2 unchanged; for layer 0, no block carries less than its P_0 where the catalog gives the flow's own count, and under a block total read from an AL-FEC message (below) a block before it whose packets carry less was generated under a previous total, which every packet of it carries, those of layer 0's own track included. Layer 0 has no clause of its own track: its O_0 is 0 and its symbols' coordinates depend on no published count, so a catalog whose layer 0 carries a block total read from an AL-FEC message rather than the flow's own count ( Section 12.2), or that message held in place of a catalog (Section 12), under which a packet of that track generated under a previous total carries less, fails a receiver closed on no conforming packet. Within a consumer protected under a flow of the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2, whether or not that profile governs it for its blocks (Section 7.4), the packet that anchors the check and the packet it tests are both repair packets that profile has admitted (step 2 of its Section 7.2.7): a symbol of an unlisted track reaches the consumer under the integrity protection of a MoQ unicast path, which vouches for the relay and not for the publisher, so the total it carries attests to no coordinate the publisher is using; it anchors nothing, and one whose RSB_length is below the O_i + P_i of a layer the receiver holds is discarded, leaving the state of every block unchanged, so that a relay on that path cannot stop FEC for the source track with one packet.

A publisher MUST NOT renumber the repairLayer of a published layer, and MUST NOT change the repairSymbols of a published layer, while any receiver may still be consuming the source track. Rule 2 of Section 6.3.4 requires repairLayer to be contiguous from 1 to n, so withdrawing a layer that is not the highest would force exactly such a renumbering. A publisher that must retire any layer, including the highest, retires the source encoding and publishes a separate rendition. Supporting withdrawal directly would require a catalog generation identifier carried on the wire, that is in-session signaling, which Section 5.2 does not define.

The prohibition is not editorial, and the worked catalog of Section 5.1.2 shows why. A receiver holding layers 0 and 2 holds, for a full block, ESIs 64 to 71 and 88 to 119. Renumber layer 2 to layer 1 and the same track's offset becomes O = 8, so the publisher now labels those symbols ESI 72 to 103 while the receiver still maps them to 88 to 119. The receiver feeds correctly received symbols into the decoder under wrong coordinates. Neither code of this document detects this, because a repair symbol is identified by its ESI alone: the result is not a reported error but a decode that fails, or that resolves against coordinates the symbols do not belong to. Changing a published repairSymbols does the same to every layer above the one changed.

Withdrawing the highest layer forces no renumbering, but it is barred for a different reason: it is indistinguishable on the wire from the renumbering above. For the highest layer n, O_n + P_n is the total identically, so withdrawing it drops the wire RSB_length strictly below the bound derived by every receiver that had joined it, and the check below cannot tell that case from a genuine coordinate disagreement. Both present as nothing but a smaller total. The receivers holding the highest layer are also the lossiest ones, and they cannot recover by observation: absence of symbols is precisely the loss condition the layer was joined to repair, so but for the check below, which fails closed those of them that hold a layer below it, on the smaller total the packets of that layer carry, they would learn of the withdrawal only at the next catalog refresh, which this document does not bound, as one holding the withdrawn layer alone, which no packet reaches after the withdrawal, does.

Append-only is what makes the check below sound. RSB_length is monotonically non-decreasing over the lifetime of a source encoding in the order blocks are generated, and a symbol of a layer above 0 is generated only under a total at or above that layer's O_i + P_i, so a wire RSB_length below a held layer's O_i + P_i on a packet of that layer's track, the layer being above 0, or on a block at or after one that carried that O_i + P_i, is always a genuine violation: no operation this document defines produces one.

A receiver MUST fail closed when, for any layer i it holds, the RSB_length carried on a repair packet of that layer's track, i being above 0, or on a repair packet of the same FEC instance of a block at or after, in the serial order of Section 7.5, one of which it has received a repair packet carrying at least O_i + P_i, is less than the O_i + P_i derived from its own catalog, or from the AL-FEC message for a receiver that holds layer 0 under that message alone (Section 12): its own layer's RS_ID range does not fit under the bound the publisher is advertising, so the two disagree about coordinates the receiver is actively using. It MUST NOT treat such a packet as a symbol to discard. In the renumbering example above the total falls from 56 to 40 while the receiver's O_2 + P_2 is 56, so the check catches it on the first packet of layer 2 it receives after the change, whenever it joined.

That check is a backstop and not a substitute for the publisher requirement. It does not catch a change that leaves the total at or above the receiver's derived bound, for example an increase to a lower layer's repairSymbols, which shifts every higher offset while raising the total. Nor does it catch, for a receiver that joins a withdrawn highest layer under a catalog that still lists it, the withdrawal itself unless a block generated while the layer was published, after its append and before the withdrawal, reaches it: no packet of that layer is generated after the withdrawal, the packets of the layers below carry, on every block generated after it, a total below O_i + P_i, which anchors the check on none of them, and their coordinates are unchanged by the withdrawal, so a receiver that takes no such block decodes from the layers below and learns of the withdrawal only at the next catalog refresh, while one that takes a packet of such a block, by the routes of the append paragraph above, whose packets carry that O_i + P_i, has the check anchored and, where it holds a layer below the withdrawn one, fails closed on the first block generated after the withdrawal that reaches it, as a receiver that had joined the layer and holds one below it does, while one holding the withdrawn layer alone, which no repair packet reaches after the withdrawal, learns of it at that refresh as well. The first case is silent on the wire, and the second where no such block arrives or the receiver holds the withdrawn layer alone, which is why the protection is the prohibition on the publisher rather than validation at the receiver. A wire RSB_length larger than the receiver's derived total is not an error in itself: that is the append case above.

section.name: Keyframe Overlay
section.t: A source track MAY additionally be protected by a keyframe overlay: a second, independent FEC instance whose source symbols are only the fragments of Random Access Points of that source track. The overlay is defined only for a source track under iso-ssbg1-v1, because its membership and its overlay SS_ID rely on the MMTP RAP_flag and header extension (Sections 6.4.2 and 8.5.1).

Losing part of a Random Access Point makes every dependent frame undecodable until the next one; the overlay protects RAP fragments across a block of its own, which can be wider than the base window, without changing the base instance's latency.

section.name: Overlay Instance
section.t: An overlay is a separate FEC instance over the same source track. It has its own sourceSymbols (K_overlay) and its own repairSymbols, declared on its own repair track, and it shares the source track's algorithm, blockProfile and symbolSize. It does not share the base instance's K, its block partition, its SS_ID space, or its RS_ID space.

Every per-block quantity of this document -- K, the total repair count P, SS_ID, ESI, RS_ID, SS_Start, RSB_length, SSB_length, the short-block rules of Section 7.4, the wrap epoch and repair group IDs of Section 7.5, and the bounds of Section 6.3.4 -- is defined within one FEC instance.
