For the base instance, K is the source track's fec.sourceSymbols and P is the sum of repairSymbols over its published layers (Section 6.3.2); for an overlay, K and P are the sourceSymbols and repairSymbols of its own track. A repair packet belongs to the instance of the track it arrived on (Section 6.4.2).

An overlay is not a repair layer. It carries no repairLayer, it is not a member of the layer index chain, and it is excluded from the contiguity and priority monotonicity rules of Section 6.3.4, which order the base layer chain only. Its priority is independent within 192 to 255, and MAY be numerically lower than a base enhancement layer's so that a keyframe repair symbol is delivered before an ordinary one.

Overlay ESIs never collide with base ESIs because the two are different instances decoded by different decoders; a receiver MUST NOT feed a repair symbol of one instance to the decoder of the other, and MUST NOT reuse a source symbol's coordinate in one instance as its coordinate in the other. A RAP source packet is a source symbol of both instances, at an unrelated coordinate in each (Section 6.4.2).

A source track has at most one overlay (Section 6.3.4, rule 10), a wire constraint explained in Section 8.5.1. An overlay is declared only by the catalog, never in an in-band AL-FEC message, and only where no FEC source or repair packet carries FFSRP_TS (Section 8.5.1).

Under reed-solomon the overlay has its own bound: K_overlay + P_overlay is at most 255 (Section 6.3.4, rule 12), whatever the base instance uses, and its rows and columns of A are numbered within the overlay instance (Section 4.5). The overlay of the worked catalog of Section 5.1.2, with K_overlay 256 and P_overlay 32, is valid only under raptorq. Under reed-solomon, an overlay whose track declares sourceSymbols 192 and repairSymbols 32 is valid, since 192 + 32 = 224.

section.name: Overlay Membership
section.t: The overlay's source symbols are the fragments of the source track that belong to a Random Access Point, in transmission order. A publisher that declares an overlay MUST set RAP_flag on a source packet of the track, MUST include the packet in the overlay instance, and MUST carry the packet's overlay SS_ID in its 0x8B01 header extension (Section 8.5.1), if and only if that packet's payload belongs to a keyframe MFU covered by the overlay.

Overlay source symbols are numbered consecutively within the overlay instance, in the order the publisher emits them: the overlay SS_ID is 0 at the first overlay source symbol of the stream and advances by one per overlay source symbol, modulo 2^32 (Section 7.5). It is the value the RAP source packet carries in its 0x8B01 header extension (Section 8.5.1). It lives in the overlay instance's own SS_ID space, independent of the base instance's, and the two IDs on one packet are unrelated numbers. An overlay source block holds at most K_overlay overlay source symbols, and overlay blocks, including short ones, are formed, located and wrapped exactly as base blocks are (Sections 7.4, 7.5 and 8.3), with K_overlay as the upper bound on their SSB_length. Because a RAP is a small fraction of the media, an overlay block spans many base blocks; the overlay's recovery latency is therefore its own block span and is unrelated to interleaveDepthMs.

A receiver knows that a source packet is an overlay source symbol because the packet carries the 0x8B01 header extension (Section 8.5.1). It knows that a repair packet belongs to the overlay because it arrives on the repair track that the catalog declares with "scope": "keyframe" for this source track, and that track has its own packet_id. The instance is therefore fixed by the track the packet arrived on; no field of the repair packet distinguishes the two, and a receiver MUST NOT attempt to infer the instance from SS_Start, RSB_length, or SSB_length, whose values are only interpretable once the instance is known.

section.name: Receiver Behavior
section.t: A receiver that implements overlays and has joined the overlay repair track decodes the two instances independently and MAY use the recovered RAP fragments even when the base instance failed to recover the block that carried them.

The overlay is the publisher-side half of keyframe protection. The receiver-side half is the repair policy of Section 11.4, under which a receiver gives a keyframe-bearing base block that in-band decoding leaves unrecovered priority unicast repair; Section 11.4.6 states how the two combine.

A receiver that does not implement overlays MUST fail closed on a catalog that declares one for a track it intends to consume, that is on a fec-repair track carrying the unknown scope key, and MUST NOT ignore the key and consume the source track anyway. This is one of the unknown-key exceptions of Section 5.1.1: a receiver that ignored the key could not tell the overlay's repair track from a repair layer of the base instance, and would feed the base decoder repair symbols of another FEC instance (Section 6.4.2).

This mechanism is not backward compatible with receivers that predate it, for the same reason. A publisher that must serve such receivers publishes the overlay on a separate source track, or does not publish it.

section.name: Repair Object Header
section.t: Under iso-ssbg1-v1, each object on a repair track is one complete MMTP repair packet (packet type 0x03, FEC Type 2) carrying exactly one repair symbol. Its layout is the ISO 23008-1 AL-FEC repair packet form -- the MMTP packet header followed by the 13-byte Repair FEC Payload ID and the repair symbol data ( Sections C.4.3 and C.5.3; ssbg_mode1, one-stage FEC with N = 1, and ffsrpts_flag = 0, so no FFSRP_TS, Section C.5.1) -- so the same repair packet is valid on MoQ, multicast UDP, and native broadcast paths without translation, and matches the repair-object depiction of Section 7. The layout below reproduces Section C.5.3 for convenience. Under moq-object-v1 a repair object is the Repair FEC Payload ID and the repair symbol alone, with no MMTP header (Section 7.6.3); every field below except the MMTP Packet Header applies under both profiles:

MMTP Packet Header: The standard 12-byte MMTP packet header ( Section 3.1) with packet type 0x03 (repair) and FEC Type 2; its packet_id routes the repair flow. Like every packet of its MMTP packet flow, source and signaling packets included, a repair packet has the packet counter flag C = 0 ( Section 3.1; Clause 9.2.3). A repair packet MUST NOT carry a header extension (X = 0). Because C = 0 and X = 0, the Repair FEC Payload ID always begins at byte offset 12.

SS_Start (32 bits): The SS_ID of the first source symbol of the protected source block ( Section C.5.3). The blocks of an FEC instance are consecutive: the block after this one starts at SS_Start + SSB_length, modulo 2^32 (Section 7.4), so this block is the SS_ID range [SS_Start, SS_Start + SSB_length) and is identified by its SS_Start. Extended to 62 bits, SS_Start is also the MoQ Group ID of the block's repair objects (Section 7.5). Every field below is that of the packet's FEC instance (Section 6.4.1).

RSB_length (24 bits): The number of repair symbols generated for the block: the instance's total repair count P when the block's repair symbols are generated, identical on every repair packet of the block. A layer does not carry its own P_i. The value rises when a layer is appended (Section 6.3.9).

RS_ID (24 bits): The zero-based index of this repair symbol among the block's P repair symbols. The Encoding Symbol ID is derived as ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID (Section 7.2): under raptorq it is the RFC 6330 Encoding Symbol ID, and under reed-solomon the code takes the symbol's column of A from RS_ID alone (Section 4.5). Layer i of the base instance carries RS_ID in [O_i, O_i + P_i) (Section 6.3.2).

Every repair symbol of a block, on whichever layer it travels, is a symbol of the one code over that block: the symbol at RS_ID r is the repair symbol that the instance's algorithm defines for r (Section 7.2). The encoder generates the instance's total repair count for each source block and assigns the disjoint RS_ID ranges to the layer tracks according to O_i. It MUST NOT encode a layer as if it were the block's only repair, for example by generating the first P_i repair symbols of the block and labeling them from O_i: those are not the block's symbols at the RS_IDs they carry, so a receiver holding more than one layer could not combine them, which is the property Section 6.3.2 depends on.

SSB_length (24 bits): The number of source symbols in the protected source block ( Section C.5.3), from 1 to K, where K is the instance's sourceSymbols (Section 5.1); it is K for a full block. It is authoritative for the block: its repair ESIs start at SSB_length (Section 7.2). Under raptorq the block is a RaptorQ source block of SSB_length source symbols, whose decoder is configured with F = SSB_length x T (Section 4.2), and under reed-solomon it is the number of rows of A that the block uses (Section 4.5). A value below K marks a short source block, to which this document's framing adds no padding symbols (Section 7.4). A publisher MUST NOT send 0 or a value above K; a receiver discards a repair packet carrying either (Section 7.4).

Repair Symbol Data: Exactly one repair symbol of Symbol Size (T) bytes, generated per Section 7.2. Carrying one symbol per object aligns the loss unit with the FEC symbol (Section 11.3) and requires no symbol-count field.

section.name: Repair Symbols
section.t: For RaptorQ, repair symbols are generated per Section 5.3. The source symbols of a block occupy ESIs 0 to SSB_length - 1 in SS_ID order, and the Encoding Symbol ID (ESI) of a repair symbol starts at SSB_length, the block's K in the notation of ( Section 5.3.1): ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID, both fields taken from the Repair FEC Payload ID (Section 7.1). The Internal Symbol IDs of , which start the repair symbols at that document's K', are internal to its encoder and decoder and never appear on the wire.

For Reed-Solomon, repair symbols are generated per Section 4.4. Source and repair symbols carry the same ESIs as under RaptorQ, so ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID still identifies a repair symbol within its block, but the code takes the symbol's column of A from its RS_ID alone (Section 4.5).
Repair symbol generation for other registered algorithms (Section 4.3) is not specified by this document.

section.name: Sub-Blocks and ssbg_mode
section.t: Per ISO 23008-1 Section C.3.3 (signalled per C.6.3, Table C.5), the FEC block structure is described by the source symbol block generation (SSBG) mode (ssbg_mode). The iso-ssbg1-v1 block profile (Section 5.1) uses ssbg_mode1, with the one-stage FEC coding structure and FEC payload ID mode 0 ( Clause C.1). This subsection specifies the source symbols of iso-ssbg1-v1; Section 7.6 specifies those of moq-object-v1.

ssbg_mode1: One MMTP source packet = one source symbol, which records the packet's length. Each MoQ object or multicast UDP datagram carries exactly one FEC symbol. Repair symbols are exactly T bytes on the wire; a SOURCE packet MAY be shorter than T on the wire -- the length field and the zero padding that complete its T-byte source symbol are applied by the encoder and decoder as part of the source symbol construction below and are NOT transmitted. This is the natural model for MMTP because packets are sized to fit in UDP datagrams and no fragmentation or reassembly is needed at the FEC layer. Every source symbol is exactly T bytes, so a block of SSB_length source symbols is exactly SSB_length x T bytes -- the property the derived Transfer Length of Section 4.2 relies on. This is ssbg_mode1 of , not ssbg_mode0, which carries no length and requires every packet of the flow to be exactly one symbol long.

Source symbol construction: The protected packet of an FEC source packet is the complete MMTP packet -- the MMTP packet header, including any header extension, followed by the MMTP payload -- before its 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID is appended ( Section C.4.2; Section 8.5). Its T-byte source symbol is ( Section C.3.3):

The Length field is in network byte order and every Padding octet is zero, so the largest protected packet a symbol can carry is T - 2 octets. A publisher MUST size every FEC source packet so that its protected packet does not exceed T - 2 octets. A receiver that observes a source packet whose protected packet exceeds T - 2 octets MUST NOT feed it to the decoder -- a truncated symbol would corrupt recovery for the entire block -- but MAY still deliver the packet as media. On a RAP packet under a keyframe overlay (Section 6.4), the base and the overlay instance form the symbol from the same protected packet, so the two protect one identical T-byte symbol.

Recovery yields the block's SSB_length source symbols. From each, the receiver takes the Length octets that follow the Length field as the recovered protected packet, and delivers that packet to the MMTP parser. A receiver MUST NOT deliver a recovered symbol whose Length is less than 12, the size in bytes of the MMTP packet header ( Section 3.1), or points past the end of the symbol, or whose Padding octets are not all zero: each means that the symbol is not the one the publisher encoded.

A recovered packet carries no Source FEC Payload ID, of either instance: the trailer is appended after FEC encoding and is not part of the protected packet. A receiver MUST NOT re-append a trailer before delivering the recovered packet to the MMTP parser, and MUST NOT expect the recovered bytes to end in a block coordinate. This holds identically for a symbol recovered by a keyframe overlay, which the receiver delivers as media on the strength of the overlay recovery alone. The 0x8B01 header extension of a RAP packet under an overlay (Section 8.5.1) is part of the protected packet, by contrast, and is recovered with it.

The packet's base SS_ID was in the trailer, and this document defines no mapping from an overlay coordinate to a base one: a receiver MUST NOT place an overlay-recovered symbol into a base source block unless it has determined that packet's base SS_ID independently. Absent that, an overlay recovery is usable as media but MUST NOT be counted toward base block recovery, and in particular MUST NOT be treated as reducing the number of erasures the base decoder still has to solve. The other direction needs no such determination, because a RAP packet recovered by the base instance still carries its overlay SS_ID (Section 8.5.1).

In-band signaling: An AL-FEC message ( Section 8.3) that describes a track under iso-ssbg1-v1 carries the coding byte 0x14: fec_coding_structure 0001 (one-stage), ssbg_mode 01, ffsrpts_flag 0 (no FFSRP_TS) and fec_payload_id_mode 0 (a Source FEC Payload ID is appended to every FEC source packet), in that bit order, per Table C.3 of as replaced by . A message carrying any other value for such a track contradicts the catalog (Section 5.2).

Sub-blocks: When a source block is too large to decode in the decoder's working memory, RFC 6330 permits dividing each block into N sub-blocks (the Number of Sub-Blocks field of the OTI). The derived OTI of Section 4.2 fixes N = 1, so catalog-signaled sessions do not use sub-blocks; the AL-FEC message of carries no OTI, and the split source blocks of its Clause C.2.2 are the two-stage coding structure, which this document does not use. A publisher using MMTP packaging under iso-ssbg1-v1 therefore uses ssbg_mode1 without sub-blocks, and never ssbg_mode2.

section.name: Short Source Blocks
section.t: A publisher MUST close a source block when it has assigned K source symbols to it. Under moq-object-v1 a block holds whole objects, so the publisher also closes it before an object that does not fit (Section 7.6.2). It MAY close a source block earlier, for example at an access-unit, media-unit, or MoQ Group boundary, or to keep the actual source/repair send span within a positive interleaveDepthMs when that field is present (Section 5.1). Such a block is a short source block, and it is a block with a smaller source symbol count: every block holds SSB_length source symbols, 1 <= SSB_length <= K ( Section C.5.3), and K -- the catalog sourceSymbols, carried in band as maximum_k_for_repair_flow under iso-ssbg1-v1 -- is an upper bound on SSB_length, not the size of any particular block. A short block differs from a full one only in SSB_length:

li.t: The publisher encodes the block as a block of its SSB_length source symbols, at ESIs 0 to SSB_length - 1 in SS_ID order: under raptorq a RaptorQ source block with F = SSB_length x T (Section 4.2), and under reed-solomon the first SSB_length rows of A (Section 4.4). It MUST carry that count in the SSB_length field of every repair packet of the block, on every repair track of the instance. This document's framing adds no padding symbols to the block: none is transmitted, and none is counted in SSB_length or F. The padding of the block to K' symbols in the notation of ( Section 5.3.1) is part of RaptorQ encoding and decoding, performed inside the encoder and the decoder.
The next block starts at the SS_ID that follows the block's last source symbol: its SS_Start is SS_Start + SSB_length, modulo 2^32. No SS_ID is skipped, so every SS_ID belongs to exactly one block.
The block's repair ESIs start at SSB_length: ESI = SSB_length + RS_ID (Section 7.2).

The block is complete, and needs no repair, once the receiver holds all SSB_length of its source symbols. It is recoverable once the source and repair symbols the receiver holds together number at least SSB_length, plus the decoding overhead of Section 6.3.2, which is zero under reed-solomon.
Recovery yields the SSB_length source symbols, SSB_length x T bytes, each consumed per the track's block profile (Sections 7.3 and 7.6.4).

section.t: Source packets and source objects carry only SS_ID, so the (SS_Start, SSB_length) of a repair packet is the only wire signal of a block's extent. Until a receiver has accepted a repair packet of a block it knows neither: it holds the source packets or objects of that block without placing them in any block (Section 8.3), and a run of SS_IDs that it does not hold is a run of lost source packets or objects of one or more blocks it cannot yet delimit. It MUST NOT infer a block boundary, or SSB_length, from a gap in SS_IDs, from a group or MPU boundary, from elapsed time, or from sourceSymbols. A block all of whose repair packets are lost therefore remains undelimited until a repair packet of the block arrives, including one obtained by unicast repair (Section 11.4), which conveys (SS_Start, SSB_length) in the same way. When the receiver accepts a repair packet of a block that starts after the end of the blocks it has delimited, the SS_IDs between the two belong to one or more blocks of which it holds no repair packet.

A receiver MUST fail closed on inconsistent block signaling. It MUST discard a repair packet whose SSB_length is 0 or exceeds K. It MUST discard a repair packet whose SSB_length differs from the value it has already accepted for the block with the same SS_Start, and one whose range [SS_Start, SS_Start + SSB_length) overlaps a different block that it has already accepted, in each case leaving the state of every block unchanged. Under reed-solomon it also discards a repair packet that fails the checks of Section 4.5.

Within a consumer that the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2 governs for its blocks, one protected under a flow whose endpoint lists its source track (step 2 of its Section 7.2.7; a consumer protected under no such flow, as one a repair-only endpoint feeds while the receiver takes the source track over MoQ unicast alone, is for this paragraph, Section 9 and Section 11.4 a consumer outside that profile, while the scoping of the check of Section 6.3.9 to admitted packets reaches it where it is protected under any flow of the profile, as it reaches every consumer so protected), a block that only symbols of an unlisted track have delimited (a track that no endpoint of a flow the consumer is protected under lists, as that step defines it: one no multicast endpoint the receiver holds lists, holding being joined to its group, reading its manifest track or receiving the broadcast that carries the flow, or one a held endpoint lists while the consumer is not yet protected under its flow; Section 6.3.6) is provisional: it yields to a repair packet the profile has admitted whose (SS_Start, SSB_length) conflicts with it, as that step specifies, and the rules of the previous paragraph then apply among admitted packets. A provisional block is held for decoding only: it has no ts and no FEC deadline (Section 9), and the SS_IDs in its range that the receiver lacks belong, for Section 11.4, to blocks the receiver holds no repair packet of, as if the block were not delimited; such a symbol reveals no run of lost SS_IDs, which a packet the profile admits above them alone reveals.

section.name: SS_ID Wrap and Repair Group IDs
section.t: SS_ID and SS_Start are 32-bit values that start from an arbitrary value and wrap to 0 after their maximum ( Section C.5.2). Every comparison, distance and range test on them in this document, block membership (Section 8.3) included, uses serial number arithmetic with SERIAL_BITS = 32. A block can span the wrap: a block with SS_Start 2^32 - 3 and SSB_length 4 holds the SS_IDs 2^32 - 3, 2^32 - 2, 2^32 - 1 and 0, and the next block starts at SS_ID 1.
The groups of a track are ordered by Group ID , so the repair objects of a block are grouped not under its 32-bit SS_Start, which wraps, but under its 62-bit extended SS_Start:
section.artwork: ext(SS_Start) = (wrap_epoch << 32) | SS_Start
section.t: wrap_epoch, from 0 to 2^30 - 1, counts the times that SS_Start has wrapped in the FEC instance before this block: it is 0 for the first block of the FEC instance's source encoding, and increases by one at each block whose SS_Start is numerically below its predecessor's. Equivalently, the ext(SS_Start) of a block is that of its predecessor plus the predecessor's SSB_length. On every repair track of the instance, the repair objects of a block form the MoQ Group whose Group ID is the block's ext(SS_Start) (Section 6.3.2). Repair Group IDs are therefore sparse, one per block at the block's first SS_ID, and strictly increasing.

MoQ Transport Group IDs range up to 2^64 - 1 ( Section 8.1). This document deliberately uses only [0, 2^62), the Group ID range of the MoQ Transport versions before draft-17, whose variable-length integers were those of QUIC (Section 5.3), so that a repair Group ID is representable in the Group ID encoding of every MoQ Transport version. The bound is not reached in practice: at one million source symbols per second, an FEC instance takes more than 100,000 years to use 2^62 SS_IDs.

Sparse Group IDs depart from the recommendation of Section 6.1 that each subsequent Group ID of a track increase by 1. The departure is deliberate: a Group ID that names its block's first SS_ID is what lets a receiver that has lost source packets request the block's repair by Group (below) before it knows the block partition. Within one source encoding the Group IDs still increase monotonically, as that section requires. A publisher MAY carry the PRIOR_GROUP_ID_GAP Object Property ( Section 10.8) on the repair objects of a block, set to the SSB_length of the preceding block of the instance minus 1. Relays and receivers that do not parse repair objects can then tell the Group IDs that will never exist from groups that have not arrived.

That section also requires a track's Group IDs to keep increasing across a publisher restart. A publisher that keeps its FEC state across a restart, for example after a loss of connectivity, continues the source encoding, with the SS_ID sequence and wrap_epoch of each FEC instance, so its repair Group IDs keep increasing. A publisher that starts a new source encoding of a track, including after a restart that loses its FEC state, retires the previous encoding and publishes a separate rendition, as Section 6.3.9 requires for retiring a layer. It MUST publish the source track and every repair track of its FEC instances under Full Track Names that it has not used before in the scope ( Section 2.5), and MUST NOT resume a previously used repair Track Name with wrap_epoch reset to 0. A resumed name would reissue Group IDs below 2^32. Repair objects of the new encoding could then take the Locations of repair objects already published, which Section 2.1 does not allow, and a receiver could feed a cached repair object of the old encoding to the decoder of a block of the new one.

A repair object received over MoQ thus carries its block's start twice: in the SS_Start of its Repair FEC Payload ID and in its Group ID. The SS_Start is authoritative. A receiver MUST discard a repair object whose Group ID modulo 2^32 differs from its SS_Start and, once it has established the wrap epoch, one whose Group ID differs from ext(SS_Start) or whose SS_Start it cannot extend (below), in each case leaving the state of every block unchanged. The Group ID of a discarded repair object is not a reference value r.
A receiver establishes the wrap epoch of an FEC instance in one of the following ways, and MUST NOT assume a wrap epoch that it has not established in one of them:

li.t: From the Group ID of a repair object of the instance that it has received over MoQ and not discarded (above). That Group ID is the reference value r. The publisher assigns it and MoQ delivers it unaltered, so it stands on the same footing as the Largest Object of way 2: the modulo 2^32 test above screens out an object to discard, and does not verify the epoch.

From the Largest Object ( Section 3.1.4) that a TRACK_STATUS request for a repair track of the instance reports ( Section 9.13). The publisher answers TRACK_STATUS with a REQUEST_OK, which that document calls TRACK_STATUS_OK, carrying the parameters that it would set in a SUBSCRIBE_OK, among them the LARGEST_OBJECT parameter ( Section 9.20.17). The receiver reads the Group of the Location that LARGEST_OBJECT carries, whichever name the reply bears, and that Group is the reference value r. A reply without LARGEST_OBJECT reports a repair track on which no object has been published, and establishes no epoch.
As epoch 0, when the receiver has observed the instance from its first block, whose wrap_epoch is 0 (above). The reference value r is then that block's SS_Start.

section.t: A reference value r is an extended SS_Start, and the epoch is r shifted right by 32 bits. The receiver relates its own SS_IDs to it with serial arithmetic: it extends a later 32-bit SS_Start or SS_ID x relative to an extended value r that it already holds -- its reference value, or a value it extended before -- to the 62-bit value congruent to x modulo 2^32 that is nearest r in serial order: r advanced by the serial distance from the low 32 bits of r to x when x follows them, r moved back by the serial distance from x to them when x precedes them, and r itself when the two are equal. A receiver MUST NOT extend an x that lies exactly 2^31 from the low 32 bits of r, a pair that leaves unordered, or one whose extension falls outside [0, 2^62).

Serial arithmetic cannot detect an x that lies more than 2^31 SS_IDs from r: it extends such an x into the wrong epoch without error. A receiver therefore extends values relative to an r only while it can bound the number of SS_IDs between them below 2^31, and MUST re-establish the wrap epoch, in one of the ways above, after any gap that it cannot so bound, such as one that spans a rejoin of a multicast group or a reconnection of its MoQ session.
A receiver that has lost the source symbol with SS_ID x, and holds no repair packet of the block that contains x, requests that block's repair by a FETCH of the absolute, inclusive Group range
section.artwork: [ max(ext(S_prev) + 1, ext(x) - (K - 1)), ext(x) ]
section.t: on each repair track it requests from, where:

ul.li: S_prev is the SS_Start of the last block that the receiver has delimited that ends before x. Within a consumer that the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2 governs for its blocks (Section 7.4), only a block that a repair packet the profile has admitted delimits counts here: a provisional block, one that only symbols of an unlisted track (Section 7.4) have delimited, is no such block, as its (SS_Start, SSB_length) is unverified and the block that contains x may start within its range. When the receiver has delimited no such block, the first term is absent and the range is [ max(ext(x) - (K - 1), 0), ext(x) ];
ext(x) is x extended relative to ext(S_prev) when S_prev exists, and otherwise relative to the reference value r of the receiver's wrap epoch.

section.t: Repair Group IDs sit at block starts, so the range returns the repair of every block that starts within it, up to and including the block that contains x, and the last Group it returns is that block. The range is never empty: it always contains ext(x). A receiver that has not established the wrap epoch, or that may not extend x, has no range to request until it establishes one. A receiver that holds a repair packet of the block requests the one Group ext(SS_Start) instead.

Each such FETCH carries a LOCATION_FILTER parameter ( Section 9.20.9). For the range [lo, hi] above, it has type 0x03 (Absolute Start, Group End), StartGroup lo, StartObject 0 and EndGroupDelta hi - lo. For the one Group ext(SS_Start), it has type 0x03 with StartGroup ext(SS_Start), StartObject 0 and EndGroupDelta 0, or, when it requests only some of the Group's objects (Section 11.4.2), type 0x04 (Absolute Range) with StartGroup ext(SS_Start), StartObject the first and EndObject the last Object ID that it requests (an inclusive range, Section 3.3.1), and EndGroupDelta 0.
The 32-bit wrap of SS_ID and SS_Start is that of . The extended SS_Start, and its use as a MoQ Group ID, are defined by this document, outside .

section.name: Object Block Profile
section.t: The moq-object-v1 block profile (Section 5.1) protects source tracks whose packaging is loc or cmaf . Its unit of protection is a whole MoQ object, not an MMTP packet. Each source object becomes one Protected Object Unit, which occupies one or more consecutive source symbols. The construction follows the application data unit framing of Section 5, with fields sized for MoQ objects.

This section defines what differs from iso-ssbg1-v1: how source symbols are formed from objects, how SS_IDs are assigned to them, how blocks are delimited around them, the form of a repair object, and how a receiver rebuilds objects from recovered symbols. The rest applies unchanged: the catalog fields (Section 5.1), the FEC Source Info Property (Section 5.3), repair layers (Section 6.3), the Repair FEC Payload ID (Section 7.1), repair symbol generation (Section 7.2), short blocks (Section 7.4), SS_ID wrap, repair Group IDs and repair FETCH (Section 7.5), and source symbol location and deduplication (Section 8.3). The profile fixes only the source symbols and their identifiers, so it does not depend on fec.algorithm: the algorithm encodes a block of this profile as it encodes any other block of SSB_length T-byte source symbols.

section.name: Protected Object Unit
section.t: A source object of a track under this profile is an object of the track whose Object Status is Normal ( Section 11.1.1). An object of any other status carries no Properties ( Section 11.1.2) and no source symbol, and is not counted in K or in any block.
The Protected Object Unit of a source object o is:
section.artwork: Protected Object Unit { Group ID (64), Object ID (64), Immutable Properties Length (16), Immutable Properties (..), Payload Length (32), Payload (..), }
section.t: All integers are unsigned and in network byte order.

ul.li: Group ID and Object ID: the Location of o ( Section 8.2).
Immutable Properties Length: the length in bytes of the value of o's Immutable Properties Property ( Section 10.7), or 0 when o has none. A Property value has at most 2^16 - 1 bytes ( Section 8.3).
Immutable Properties: that value, the Key-Value-Pairs exactly as the publisher serialized them, which no node may change ( Section 10.7). It is empty when the length is 0.
Payload Length: the length in bytes of the Object Payload of o.
Payload: the Object Payload of o.

section.t: The fields are fixed-width for the reason Section 5.3 gives for SS_ID: a variable-length integer has several valid encodings, so using one here would make the unit depend on the encoding that a session chose. The unit is 22 bytes longer than the Immutable Properties value and the payload together.
Let len(o) be the length of the unit in bytes and T the track's symbolSize. The unit occupies
section.artwork: s(o) = ceil(len(o) / T)
section.t: source symbols. They are the unit followed by s(o) x T - len(o) zero octets, cut into s(o) consecutive T-byte symbols, so every source symbol is exactly T bytes, as Sections 4.2 and 4.5 require. Neither the fixed-width fields nor the padding is transmitted: the object travels in its usual MoQ form, and the publisher and each receiver build the unit from the object's fields. The mutable Properties, Subgroup ID, Publisher Priority and Delivery Mode of the object are not in the unit.

section.name: Source Objects and Blocks
section.t: The publisher assigns SS_IDs to source symbols in the order in which it emits source objects. Let SS_ID(o) be the SS_ID of the first source symbol of o. The unit of o occupies the s(o) SS_IDs from SS_ID(o) on, and the next source object o' that the publisher emits starts where o ends:
section.artwork: SS_ID(o') = (SS_ID(o) + s(o)) mod 2^32
section.t: The publisher MUST carry SS_ID(o) in a FEC Source Info Property (Section 5.3) on every source object o. The Property SHOULD be inside the object's Immutable Properties, where no node may change it ( Section 10.7) and where end-to-end authentication can cover it (Section 14.6). There it is also part of the unit, so it is recovered with the object (Section 7.6.4). SS_ID(o) depends only on the objects emitted before o, and the Property's value has a fixed length, so the publisher can place the Property inside the unit that it numbers.

A block holds whole units: every SS_ID of a source object lies in the block that holds its first SS_ID, so SSB_length is the sum of s(o) over the objects of the block. A publisher MUST NOT publish a source object whose s(o) exceeds K, the track's sourceSymbols. It chooses sourceSymbols and symbolSize so that the unit of its largest object fits in K x T bytes; an algorithm that allows only small blocks, such as reed-solomon with K + totalP at most 255 (Section 4.5), therefore limits the largest object a track can protect. When the open block already holds more than K - s(o) source symbols, the publisher MUST close it before it assigns SS_IDs to o, and o starts the next block (Section 7.4). The publisher MAY also close a block at any object boundary, for example at a Group boundary.

section.name: Repair Objects
section.t: Under this profile a repair object is the Repair FEC Payload ID followed by exactly one repair symbol, with no MMTP header:

The object payload is therefore 13 + T bytes long, and the Repair FEC Payload ID begins at byte offset 0. Its fields have the meanings and validity rules of Section 7.1, and the repair Group ID, Object ID and layer rules of Sections 6.3.2 and 7.5 apply unchanged. A receiver routes a repair object to the decoder of the source track that the catalog relates to the repair track it arrived on (Section 5.1.1). It MUST discard a repair object whose payload is not 13 + T bytes long.

section.name: Recovery
section.t: A receiver builds the unit of each source object it holds and places the unit's s(o) source symbols at the SS_IDs from SS_ID(o) on (Section 8.3). An object o in a block occupies ESIs ESI(o) to ESI(o) + s(o) - 1, where ESI(o) is the ESI of SS_ID(o). The receiver MUST NOT feed the decoder a source object whose s(o) exceeds K, one whose SS_IDs do not all lie in the block that holds SS_ID(o), or either of two different objects whose SS_ID ranges overlap. Each means that the object or the block signaling is not what the publisher sent. The receiver MAY still deliver such an object as media.

Decoding yields the block's source data, SSB_length x T bytes in ESI order. The receiver rebuilds the objects it lacks from each run of ESIs that no object it fed to the decoder covers. It walks each run from its first ESI, one unit at a time:

li.t: It reads Group ID, Object ID, Immutable Properties Length, Immutable Properties, Payload Length and Payload, in that order. Every byte read MUST lie inside the run.
With len the number of bytes read and s = ceil(len / T), every octet from the end of the unit to the end of its s-th symbol MUST be zero.
The next unit starts s symbols after the start of this one. The walk MUST end exactly at the end of the run.

section.t: If any of these checks fails, the receiver MUST NOT deliver any object from the run, because the run is not what the publisher encoded. It also MUST NOT deliver a rebuilt object:

ul.li: whose Immutable Properties do not parse as a sequence of Key-Value-Pairs ( Section 8.3), or contain an Immutable Properties Property ( Section 10.7);

whose Immutable Properties carry a FEC Source Info Property with a value other than the SS_ID of the unit's first symbol, which is SS_Start plus the ESI at which the walk found the unit, modulo 2^32; or
whose Location is that of an object the receiver already holds.

section.t: A failed check concerns bytes that the receiver computed, not an object that it received. The receiver discards the rebuilt data, and the failure is not a protocol error of the session.

A rebuilt object that passes these checks is the object at its Location, with the rebuilt Immutable Properties as its only Properties and the rebuilt payload as its payload. The receiver delivers it to the track's consumer and takes its SS_ID from the block coordinate (Section 5.3). The mutable Properties, Subgroup ID, Publisher Priority and Delivery Mode of the object are not recovered. MoQ Transport sends an object according to those fields ( Section 2.1.1), so an entity that rebuilds an object delivers it to its own consumer only, and MUST NOT forward it as an object of the source track.

section.name: Packaging Requirements
section.t: A rebuilt object has no mutable Properties (Section 7.6.4). On a loc track the LOC Public Properties are Object Properties ( Section 2.2), so a LOC Property is recovered only if it is inside Immutable Properties. A publisher of a loc track under this profile MUST carry inside Immutable Properties every LOC Public Property that it sets on a source object and that a receiver needs to decode or present the object. These include Timestamp and Timescale ( Section 2.3.1) and, where the track uses them, Video Config, Video Frame Marking and Audio Config ( Sections 2.3.2 and 2.3.3). Section 3.1.2 already recommends Immutable Properties for such Properties. LOC Private Properties travel in the object payload and are recovered with it.

On a cmaf track each object holds one or more successive CMAF chunks ( Section 3.3), and no chunk or CMAF Fragment spans a Group ( Section 3.4). The publisher chooses K and T so that K x T covers the largest such object (Section 7.6.2). The sample timing a receiver needs is in each chunk's movie fragment, inside the payload, so a rebuilt cmaf object is complete without Properties. The CMAF header that initializes decoding comes from the catalog ( Section 3.1), not from the objects.

An object-protection scheme can authenticate the Publisher Priority of each object, as MoQ Secure Objects does ( Section 3.5), and the unit does not carry it. A publisher that protects a track under this profile with such a scheme SHOULD give every object of the track the track's DEFAULT_PUBLISHER_PRIORITY ( Section 10.4), so that a receiver can form the authenticated data of a rebuilt object and verify it.

section.name: Applicability
section.t: The keyframe overlay (Section 6.4) is not defined for this profile. Its membership and its overlay SS_ID rely on the MMTP RAP_flag and header extension (Sections 6.4.2 and 8.5.1), which a loc or cmaf object does not have. A catalog that declares an overlay for a source track under this profile violates rule 10 of Section 6.3.4, and a receiver fails closed on it. Repair layers (Section 6.3) apply.

This profile is defined for MoQ paths only. A multicast endpoint lists only mmtp tracks, and a loc or cmaf track reaches multicast through an mmtp rendition track, which is a separate FEC instance under iso-ssbg1-v1 ( Sections 4.1 and 5). Symbols of the two tracks never combine. The receiver repair policy of Section 11.4, which serves multicast and AMT legs, does not apply to a track under this profile.

On a MoQ path the erasure unit is a whole object, not a symbol. An object sent as a datagram is dropped whole when it exceeds the maximum datagram size of a session on its path ( Section 11.2). A delivery timeout drops a datagram, or resets the subgroup stream that carries an object ( Section 5.2). A lost object erases all s(o) of its source symbols, so a block recovers its lost objects only when the repair symbols the receiver holds number at least the source symbols those objects span, plus the decoding overhead (Section 6.3.2). The profile therefore helps most with small objects, such as audio frames sent as datagrams, and with objects that a delivery timeout drops. In-band recovery of a keyframe object needs a total repair count of at least its s(o). Otherwise a receiver recovers it from a further repair layer or by a FETCH of the object, or resumes at the next Group. FEC pays off most on multicast, where one lost packet erases one symbol (Section 11.3); for a loc or cmaf track that leg is the mmtp rendition.

All source objects of a track share one SS_ID sequence. Objects that a receiver does not receive by design, such as the subgroups of a temporal layer that a relay drops under congestion, count as erasures and consume repair symbols. A layer that receivers may skip is therefore better published as a separate track with its own FEC instance, as Section 4.4 does for spatial layers.

section.name: Example
section.t: The catalog below declares a LOC video track under this profile. Each one-second Group holds one Group of Pictures (GOP): an Instantaneous Decoder Refresh (IDR) frame as Object 0 and 29 P-frames as Objects 1 to 29 ( Section 4.2). The publisher sends the parameter sets in the IDR payload ( Section 2.1.1), so the track needs no Video Config.

Each object carries 15 bytes of Immutable Properties: Timescale in 4 bytes (Delta Type 0x08 and the value 90000 in 3 bytes), Timestamp in 5 bytes (a 4-byte value) and FEC Source Info in 6 bytes. Each unit is therefore 37 bytes longer than its payload. With T = 1200:

ul.li: An IDR payload of 60,000 bytes gives len(o) = 60,037 and s(o) = 51. The unit's last symbol ends with 1,163 bytes of padding, which are not sent.
A P-frame payload of 7,000 bytes gives len(o) = 7,037 and s(o) = 6, with 163 bytes of padding.
A Group therefore spans 51 + 29 x 6 = 225 source symbols, within K = 256.

section.t: Suppose the first source object of the FEC instance, {0, 0}, has SS_ID 0, every Group so far has this shape, and the publisher closes a block at each Group boundary. Group g then starts at SS_ID 225 x g, and its block has SS_Start 225 x g and SSB_length 225. For Group 5:
Objects {5, 6} to {5, 28}, which the table omits, follow the same pattern.

Object {6, 0} starts at SS_ID 1350. The block's repair objects form Group 1125 of video/repair (Section 7.5): Objects 0 to 31, with RS_IDs 0 to 31 and ESIs 225 to 256, each 13 + 1200 = 1,213 bytes long. The block's source objects are sent over 967 ms, and its repair objects follow the last of them, so the catalog's interleaveDepthMs of 1200 covers the block's send span (Section 5.1).

Suppose a delivery timeout drops {5, 3} and {5, 4}. The receiver holds {5, 2}, which ends at SS_ID 1187, and {5, 5}, which starts at SS_ID 1200, so ESIs 63 to 74 form a run of 12 missing source symbols. With the other 213 source symbols and the 32 repair symbols it holds 245 symbols, 20 more than SSB_length, and decodes. It walks the run from ESI 63. The unit there has Group ID 5, Object ID 3, Immutable Properties Length 15 and Payload Length 7,000, so len = 7,037 and s = 6, and bytes 7,037 to 7,199 from the start of the unit must be zero. The next unit, at ESI 69, is {5, 4} with s = 6, so the walk ends at ESI 75, where {5, 5} starts, as required. The FEC Source Info values in the two units are 1188 and 1194, their first SS_IDs. The receiver delivers both objects with their Timescale, Timestamp and FEC Source Info Properties.

This block recovers the loss of up to five P-frame objects, 30 symbols, with 2 symbols of decoding overhead (Section 6.3.2). The IDR object spans 51 symbols, more than the block's 32 repair symbols, so its loss is not recovered in band: the receiver needs a further repair layer or a FETCH of the object, or resumes at the next Group.
This example uses raptorq. Its catalog is not valid under reed-solomon, since 256 + 32 exceeds 255 (Section 6.3.4, rule 12).

section.name: Block and Group Alignment
section.t: FEC blocks are partitions of the source symbol sequence, independent of MoQ Group boundaries. The publisher assigns consecutive SS_ID values to source symbols and chooses each block's SSB_length subject to 1 <= SSB_length <= K (Section 7.4). It signals the chosen partition in the (SS_Start, SSB_length) fields of the block's repair packets. A block MAY end at an access-unit, media-unit, or Group boundary, MAY span Groups, and MAY end because it reaches K. K exhaustion closes a block. A Group MAY contain more than one block. A positive interleaveDepthMs limits the elapsed source/repair send span; it does not change this partitioning rule.

section.name: Blocks Within a Group
section.t: For example, a source Group can contain two consecutive blocks:
section.artwork: Group G: SS_ID s .. s+a-1 -> block A, SS_Start = s SS_ID s+a .. s+a+b-1 -> block B, SS_Start = s+a Group G+1: SS_ID s+a+b .. -> next block or continuation ...

section.name: Blocks Across Groups
section.t: A block can also span a Group boundary:
section.artwork: Group G: SS_ID s .. s+a-1 -> block A, still open Group G+1: SS_ID s+a .. s+L-1 -> block A completes SS_ID s+L .. -> next block ...
section.t: A block's repair objects form the repair-track Group whose Group ID is the block's extended SS_Start (Section 7.5), a number space unrelated to the source track's Group IDs. No fixed number of MoQ Groups is required for a block, and no Group boundary can be used to infer SSB_length.

section.name: Source Symbol Location
section.t: Under iso-ssbg1-v1, every FEC source packet carries a Source FEC Payload ID (Section 8.5), and a receiver that parses the packet takes each source symbol's SS_ID from that field on every path that delivers the packet with its trailer. The SS_ID is also carried alongside the packet where the packaging says so: on the MoQ path every object carrying a source symbol carries it in the FEC Source Info Object Property (Section 5.3), under the same value and the same definition, whether or not that object also delivers the trailer. A receiver that does not parse the FEC source packet -- a relay, or a MoQ receiver with no MMTP parser -- takes the SS_ID from there. The SS_ID advances by one per FEC source packet, modulo 2^32, in the order the publisher emits the packets ( Section C.5.2), and the blocks of an FEC instance are consecutive: each starts at the SS_ID that follows the last source symbol of its predecessor (Section 7.4).

Under moq-object-v1, a source object carries no Source FEC Payload ID. On every MoQ path its FEC Source Info Property is the only carrier of its SS_ID, which is the SS_ID of the first source symbol of its Protected Object Unit. The SS_ID advances by s(o) per source object, modulo 2^32, in the order the publisher emits the objects (Section 7.6.2), and blocks are consecutive as under iso-ssbg1-v1.

A source symbol is located by range membership. It belongs to the block whose Repair FEC Payload ID (Section 7.1) carries an (SS_Start, SSB_length) such that the symbol's SS_ID lies in [SS_Start, SS_Start + SSB_length) under the serial arithmetic of Section 7.5, and its ESI is its serial distance from SS_Start:
section.artwork: ESI = (SS_ID - SS_Start) mod 2^32, 0 <= ESI < SSB_length
section.t: Under moq-object-v1, an object o whose first SS_ID has ESI ESI(o) occupies ESIs ESI(o) to ESI(o) + s(o) - 1 of the same block (Section 7.6.2).

No source symbol's block can be computed from its SS_ID alone, because blocks differ in length (Section 7.4), and this document defines no block number. A receiver holds a source symbol whose block it has not yet delimited, and places it when it accepts a repair packet of that block. Because SS_IDs are consecutive, a lost source packet or object is visible as missing SS_IDs even before its block is delimited, and a run of SS_IDs that a receiver holds in full needs no repair, whatever its block boundaries.

An object that a packaging profile defines as carrying no source symbol -- for example, the in-band AL-FEC signaling object of Section 8 -- carries no SS_ID, has no ESI, and is not counted in K or in any block. Under moq-object-v1 the objects that carry no source symbol are those whose Object Status is not Normal (Section 7.6.1). This document defines no derivation of a source symbol's position from MoQ Group or Object IDs, under either profile: Object IDs are not positions in the FEC block, and a packaging profile that defines source objects carrying neither a Source FEC Payload ID nor a FEC Source Info Object Property (Section 5.3) needs a block profile of its own (Section 5.1).

Under iso-ssbg1-v1, every transport path yields the same SS_ID for the same packet, because each path carries the same MMTP packet, so receivers MAY combine symbols from any transport path toward the same FEC block recovery. Under moq-object-v1, every MoQ path delivers the same object with the same FEC Source Info Property, so receivers MAY likewise combine symbols received over any MoQ path, FETCH included. A loc or cmaf track reaches multicast only through a separate mmtp rendition track ( Section 4.1), whose symbols belong to another FEC instance. Within one FEC instance (Section 6.4.1), a receiver deduplicates source symbols by SS_ID and repair symbols by (SS_Start, RS_ID).

section.name: Encoder Constraints
section.t: For FEC block alignment and timing to be deterministic, encoders MUST:

li.t: Assign consecutive SS_ID values in the order the publisher emits source packets, or under moq-object-v1 source objects (Section 7.6.2), close a block at K source symbols or earlier as permitted by Section 7.4, and publish the resulting (SS_Start, SSB_length) in every repair packet for that block. A publisher MAY close at an access-unit, media-unit, or Group boundary, but MUST NOT use any boundary or elapsed-time observation as a substitute for that wire signaling.

For mmtp-packaged tracks, signal the catalog-authored group duration and frame rate in the MoQ catalog: publish a positive duration as groupDurationMs when its integer-millisecond form is exact, or as the exact positive groupDurationTicks; when both are present, groupDurationTicks wins and groupDurationMs is informational. Signal the keyframe cadence in keyframeIntervalMs (or keyframeIntervalTicks), and the frame rate in the framerate field ( Sections 4.4.2, 4.4.3 and 12.1). The ISO 23008-1 AL-FEC message has no field for either value ( Table C.3), so an encoder signals neither there, and a receiver takes neither from it.
If frame rate or GOP size changes mid-session, update the MoQ catalog and signal a manifest discontinuity for DASH/HLS.

When interleaveDepthMs is positive, choose it so that the actual elapsed send span from the first source or repair packet of every block to its last does not exceed the signaled value. Under iso-ssbg1-v1, a zero value is usable only with the ISO protection_window_size alternative described in Section 5.1; under moq-object-v1 it is equivalent to an absent field. The value is not derived from a group count, frame count, or per-symbol interval.

section.name: Source FEC Payload ID and ATSC 3.0 Signed Region
section.t: This subsection and Section 8.5.1 apply under iso-ssbg1-v1. A source object under moq-object-v1 carries no trailer, and its FEC Source Info Property is the only carrier of its SS_ID (Section 7.6.2); Section 14.6 covers how that Property can be authenticated.

Exactly one 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID (SS_ID; ffsrpts_flag = 0, so no FFSRP_TS, Section C.5.1) is appended at the END of each MMTP FEC source packet -- following the MMTP payload, outside the MMTP packet header -- with or without a keyframe overlay (Section 8.5.1). Per Section 5.2.2.5, the ATSC 3.0 signing mechanism, whose certificates the ATSC 3.0 Security Authority (A3SA) administers, covers signaling messages and MA3 messages (packet type 0x2) but excludes asset packets (type 0x00 MPU and type 0x03 repair).

Neither nor carries the SS_ID inside the A3SA signed region. In particular the MMT hint sample does not: neither its ISO syntax ( Clause 8.3.2) nor the ATSC MMTHSampleATSC3 syntax ( Section 7.2.4.2.2.3) has a Source FEC Payload ID field, and hint samples travel as MPU-mode data units on the Asset's own packet_id ( Section 7.2.4.2.3), that is in asset packets, which A3SA does not sign. This document therefore defines no A3SA-authenticated FEC block assignment: block assignment taken from the trailing Source FEC Payload ID of an A3SA verified packet is unauthenticated. A receiver that requires authenticated FEC block assignment MUST obtain it from an integrity mechanism, other than A3SA signing, whose coverage includes the complete MMTP packet, the trailer included. Version 2 of the bc-provenance profile ( Section 7.2) is such a mechanism: its digest covers the whole UDP payload as transmitted, the Source FEC Payload ID included.

For MoQ-only receivers (no A3SA verification), the trailing 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID remains the canonical identifier by which a source packet is placed in its block (Section 8.3). QUIC transport encryption provides equivalent integrity protection.

Whatever the receiver's verification posture, the FEC Source Info Object Property of Section 5.3 carries the same value for a receiver that does not parse the packet; where an object delivers both and they disagree, the trailer is the one that is canonical, because it is the field the FEC encoder emitted and the one Section 8.3 locates the symbol by. The Property restates it at the MoQ layer.

section.name: Overlay SS_ID Header Extension
section.t: When the catalog declares a keyframe overlay for a source track (Section 6.4), a source packet of that track carrying a Random Access Point fragment is a source symbol of two FEC instances. It carries its base SS_ID in the one Source FEC Payload ID trailer that every FEC source packet carries (Section 8.5), and its overlay SS_ID (Section 6.4.2) in an MMTP header extension ( Clause 9.2.3) of type 0x8B01:

A publisher that declares an overlay MUST carry this extension as the header extension, with X = 1, of exactly the source packets that it includes in the overlay instance, that is the packets on which it sets RAP_flag (Section 6.4.2), and of no other packet of the track. An MMTP packet carries at most one header extension ( Clause 9.2.3), so the RAP packets of a track under an overlay carry no other MMTP header extension, and a publisher that needs another header extension on those packets cannot use the overlay for that track. specifies no particular header extension and no registry of header extension types; this document uses the type 0x8B01 for the overlay SS_ID (Section 15.1).

The trailer is never more than one Source FEC Payload ID. On a packet with or without the extension, the last four bytes are the base SS_ID, as Section C.4.2 places it, so a receiver that does not implement overlays locates the trailer and the payload as on any other packet, stepping over the extension by its Length field. The extension lies inside the MMTP packet header, so it is part of the protected packet of both instances (Section 7.3), which protect one identical source symbol. The permission of Clause 9.2.3 to discard a header extension therefore extends only to a receiver's own processing: a node that forwards the packet MUST NOT remove or alter the extension. A RAP packet recovered by either instance carries its overlay SS_ID, so a receiver MAY place a RAP packet that the base instance recovered into the overlay block that the extension locates; Section 7.3 states why the converse requires the packet's base SS_ID.

A receiver that implements overlays takes a packet's overlay SS_ID from this extension and from nothing else. It MUST NOT feed the overlay decoder a source packet that lacks the extension, whatever its RAP_flag, or one whose extension has a Length other than 4, and MUST NOT infer an overlay SS_ID from RAP_flag, from the packet's position, or from its base SS_ID.

A source track has at most one overlay (Section 6.3.4, rule 10) because a source packet has one header extension, and so carries one overlay SS_ID; relaxing that bound would be a revision of this document and a change to the source packet layout, not a catalog-only change.

The overlay is declared only by the catalog. A publisher MUST NOT describe the overlay's repair flow in an AL-FEC message ( Section 8.3): the message identifies an FEC source flow by packet_id ( Clause C.6.3) and cannot describe the RAP subset that the overlay protects, so a receiver that consumes the flow without the catalog uses the base instance alone. An overlay is defined only without FFSRP_TS: a publisher MUST NOT declare an overlay for a source track whose FEC source or repair packets carry FFSRP_TS (ffsrpts_flag = 1, Section C.5.1), and the extension carries an SS_ID alone.
Section 8.5 applies to the overlay SS_ID as to the base one: A3SA signing authenticates neither, and a receiver that requires authenticated block assignment treats each as Section 8.5 requires.

section.name: Interleaving
section.t: Interleaving spreads source symbols across time to protect against burst loss. The interleave window (Interleave Depth, in milliseconds) bounds the elapsed send span of a source block when the field is positive. It does not define the block's membership or imply a number of Groups. Block membership is the consecutive SS_ID range identified by (SS_Start, SSB_length) (Sections 7.4 and 8.3).
section.artwork: Groups: M0 M1 M2 | | | Blocks: [Block 0] [Block 1] [Block 2] [Block 3] SS_ID: S0 S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 S6 S7 ... | | | | Repair Groups: ext(S0) ext(S2) ext(S4) ext(S6)
section.t: A burst loss can therefore erase symbols from several adjacent blocks; each block is recovered with the repair symbols identified by its own SS_Start and SSB_length. With P repair symbols for a block, the recovery condition of the track's algorithm (Section 6.3.2) applies independently to that block.
Publishers SHOULD choose the interleave window based on:

ul.li: Expected burst loss duration
Acceptable recovery latency
Available bandwidth for repair overhead

section.t: The receiver's block-abandonment timeout -- how long it waits for a block's source and repair symbols before declaring the block unrecoverable -- follows the ISO receiver-buffer model Section 11.2. The timer is anchored at the timestamp ts of the first source or repair packet of the block when the receiver received that packet, not at block creation or the first repair receipt. A block whose first packet the receiver did not receive is one that it first learns of from a later signal -- a later source or repair packet of the block, a packet of a successor block, or a FETCH response that covers the block (Section 7.5) -- and its ts is the arrival time of that signal. Within a consumer that the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2 governs for its blocks (Section 7.4), the packet whose receipt anchors ts is the first packet of the block, in the order received, that the profile admits, whenever it admits it (a datagram held on a miss and admitted later keeps its receipt time), and a symbol of an unlisted track (Section 7.4) is neither that packet nor such a signal, whether or not a repair packet the profile admits later delimits the same block; a block that only such symbols have delimited is held for decoding only: it has no ts and no FEC deadline, whatever packets the profile admits into or above its range, and the SS_IDs in its range that the receiver lacks are runs of Section 11.4, each with the ts the packet admitted above it gives, as step 2 of Section 7.2.7 specifies. When interleaveDepthMs is positive, the base FEC deadline is:
section.artwork: base_deadline = ts + interleaveDepthMs
section.t: Here a positive interleaveDepthMs is the complete first-to-last source/repair send span of the block, which bounds source and repair production at the media cadence and their serialization. An absent value supplies no elapsed-time base deadline. Under iso-ssbg1-v1, a zero value invokes the ISO protection_window_size alternative; this catalog profile supplies no packet-count window, so a catalog-only receiver has no elapsed-time base deadline from that value. If an applicable count window is accepted in-band, it governs separate count-based processing and is not converted to milliseconds without an independently defined time mapping. Under moq-object-v1 a zero value is equivalent to an absent one.

The block assignment rule in Section 8.3 means that implementations do not derive a full-block span or an FEC deadline from K, a Group count, a per-symbol interval, or by a multiplier. When the field is positive, a deadline adds interleaveDepthMs and, where used, reorderToleranceMs, each exactly once.

A receiver uses the catalog reorderToleranceMs allowance, when present, for network jitter, one-way delay, reordering, and local processing before abandoning the block. That allowance is additive to the base span and MUST be applied exactly once. If interleaveDepthMs is absent or zero, no elapsed-time deadline is derived from this FEC window. An applicable ISO packet-count window accepted in-band governs separate count-based processing; it does not become a millisecond deadline without an independently defined time mapping. When an elapsed-time deadline exists, the receiver moves the block onward at that deadline and attempts FEC processing according to its buffering model. What a receiver of a multicast or AMT leg does with a block that is still unrecovered at that deadline -- unicast repair, a stall, or concealment -- is specified in Section 11.4.

A receiver MUST bound the state it holds for open blocks by a receiver-local policy, for example a memory cap, a local timeout, or a later block that has itself passed its FEC deadline or local timeout. The bound is needed even when no FEC deadline exists: a receiver that loses every repair packet of a block never learns its SSB_length (Section 7.4). For a block that has an FEC deadline, the policy MUST NOT discard the block before that deadline, or while a unicast repair FETCH for it is outstanding (Section 11.4.2), except under a memory cap. A block so discarded is treated from then on as having reached its FEC deadline unrecovered and, on a track whose blocks Section 11.4.1 classifies, of unknown class. Within a consumer that the bc-provenance profile governs for its blocks (Section 7.4), the policy discards a block that has no ts, one that only symbols of an unlisted track have delimited, before any block that has a ts, on a track that derives no FEC deadline as on one that does, and such a discard is neither a reached deadline nor a signal: it gives the block no deadline and no class, drops its repair symbols and returns its source symbols to the undelimited state of Section 7.4 (step 2 of Section 7.2.7). The policy is not signaled, and a receiver MUST keep it separate from the catalog values: it does not change interleaveDepthMs, reorderToleranceMs, or a deadline derived from them, and discarding a block under it does not create an FEC deadline (Section 11.4).

The code is systematic (Section 4.1): a receiver plays source objects on arrival, and the window adds latency only when a lossy leg forces it to wait for recovery. The interleaveDepthMs value is the worst-case source/repair send-span budget when it is present.

section.name: Priority and Congestion
section.t: Priorities in this document are expressed in the MoQ Transport priority scale : an 8-bit value (0-255) in which a numerically LOWER value is delivered with HIGHER precedence. Repair tracks SHOULD use a numerically greater (lower-precedence) priority than the source tracks they protect, so that repair data is dropped first under congestion. The RECOMMENDED assignment places a repair track's priority value at least 64 above its source track's (e.g. repair 240 against a source track at the common default of 128):

Layer priorities and the layer-0 default follow Section 6.3.4, rule 3, so under congestion the highest layer is shed first and a receiver degrades through its layer set in order; a keyframe overlay's priority is independent of that order (Section 6.4.1).

Publishers and relays convey these priorities through the priority fields and scheduling rules of (subscriber and publisher priority); QUIC itself defines no wire-visible stream priority mechanism. A repair track's catalog priority is the Publisher Priority of its objects, and Section 5.1.1 states how a subscriber chooses its subscriber priority for the track.
Under congestion, this priority separation ensures:

ol.li: Source media is preserved as long as possible
Repair overhead is gracefully shed
Receivers degrade to QUIC retransmission when FEC is unavailable

section.t: On a multicast or AMT leg, the priorities of on-demand unicast repair requests are set by Section 11.4.5.

section.name: Hybrid Unicast and Multicast Delivery
section.t: This FEC mechanism is designed to support hybrid delivery architectures where the same media stream is delivered via multiple transport paths simultaneously. Multicast delivery paths, TreeDN integration, and the transport hierarchy (Sections 1 and 3) are defined in ; this section covers FEC-specific considerations for hybrid delivery.

section.name: Multicast and AMT Delivery
section.t: IP multicast (including Source-Specific Multicast per ) and Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT per ) provide efficient one-to-many delivery but are inherently unreliable. FEC enables receivers to recover from packet loss without retransmission:

ul.li: Native SSM: Receivers join multicast group directly
AMT Tunneling: Receivers without native multicast connect via AMT relays discovered through DRIAD ()

TreeDN (): native SSM where a network supports multicast, and AMT relays, found through DRIAD, for receivers on unicast-only networks. The publisher generates FEC repair end to end, and the repair is the same on every leg.

section.t: For an mmtp track, the same MoQ objects (source and repair) can be transmitted over both unicast (QUIC/WebTransport) and multicast (UDP/SSM/AMT) paths. Receivers on reliable unicast paths can skip FEC decoding (Section 3), while receivers on lossy multicast paths use FEC for recovery and apply the receiver repair policy of Section 11.4 to any block that FEC does not recover. A multicast endpoint carries only mmtp tracks, so a loc or cmaf track under moq-object-v1 reaches multicast through an mmtp rendition track, which is a separate FEC instance ( Section 4.1).
