section.name: Deployment Applicability
section.t: The repair overhead this mechanism adds is justified only where the delivery path actually loses packets, and multicast loss characteristics differ by orders of magnitude across access technologies. FEC strength (P and Interleave Depth) is a per-path deployment choice, expressed by which tracks each endpoint carries, not a protocol constant.

li.t: Engineered low-loss segments. On managed PON or DOCSIS delivered over a provisioned VLAN, steady-state loss is typically far below 10^-6. Disabling FEC for such a path is signaled by omitting the repair track from the tracks that path's endpoints carry. Adding repair symbols on such a path spends bandwidth to recover losses that do not occur.

FEC-capable broadcast PHYs. ATSC 3.0, DVB-S2/S2X, and 5G broadcast already apply bit-error correction on their own radio link (e.g., LDPC/BCH in ATSC 3.0 and DVB-S2/S2X). Application-layer FEC is NOT a duplicate of that correction: it recovers packet erasures the PHY cannot address -- bursts when reception falls below the PHY threshold (rain fade, mobility, indoor reception), and losses on upstream aggregation or backbone hops that the last-hop PHY never sees. Its value on these paths comes primarily from Interleave Depth spreading a burst across the time domain, not from the code rate. On a one-way broadcast downlink with no return path, application-layer FEC is the only available erasure-recovery mechanism -- which is why ATSC 3.0 (see Section 12) specifies it above the PHY.
Public Internet and AMT tunnels. Loss is real and bursty; a non-trivial repair count with interleaving is RECOMMENDED.

section.t: A track under moq-object-v1 travels on MoQ paths only, where the erasure unit is a whole object; Section 7.6.6 states where that profile helps.

section.name: Interaction with Multicast QUIC
section.t: This subsection is informative.

lets a server send QUIC packets on one-way multicast channels. A channel is an alternate path of the unicast QUIC connections whose clients have joined it, and its packets can carry STREAM and DATAGRAM frames. Clients acknowledge channel packets with MC_ACK frames on their unicast connections ( Section 4.4). The server of each connection remains responsible for any necessary frame data that a channel loses, and Section 8 of recommends that it send FEC repair packets on the channel instead of retransmitting the lost frames. That repair is a transport mechanism below this scheme, and this document does not depend on it. This scheme can serve as the application-layer FEC on such a channel, and suits broadcast-scale audiences better than unicast repair, because per-receiver retransmission does not scale.
When this scheme is carried over a multicast QUIC channel:

li.t: Symbol-to-datagram mapping. Each source or repair symbol (one MMTP packet, per ) is best carried in exactly one QUIC DATAGRAM frame. This aligns the erasure unit (a lost QUIC packet) with the FEC symbol, so one lost packet erases exactly one source symbol. STREAM framing defeats symbol-aligned recovery of FEC-protected media on a multicast channel: a lost packet then spans a byte range crossing symbol boundaries.

Crypto boundary. FEC encoding operates on application-layer objects, ABOVE the QUIC packet protection of . Unlike bare multicast UDP -- which lacks QUIC's integrity guarantees (see Section 14.4) -- the multicast QUIC binding applies a shared-key AEAD per packet. A sender computes source and repair symbols over the unencrypted objects; the channel then applies its AEAD; a receiver decrypts each surviving packet and recovers erased objects from the decrypted source and repair symbols. A lost packet cannot be decrypted, but its object is reconstructed from other verified symbols, so recovery does not depend on possessing it.

Integrity of recovered objects. The MC_INTEGRITY frames of carry hashes of channel packets, and a client decodes a channel packet only after a matching hash has arrived over another integrity-protected path ( Section 4.5). A FEC-reconstructed object was never carried in a single packet and is therefore not individually covered by a packet hash; it inherits trust transitively from the verified surviving symbols used to reconstruct it. Deployments requiring per-object authentication of recovered data can additionally apply a scheme that authenticates every multicast symbol before it enters the decoder, repair symbols included, and, whenever a symbol of its decode was not so authenticated, checks a recovered packet against its own digest or, where it can derive no coordinate to hash with, withholds it (for example version 2 of the manifest-based bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2, whose receiver procedure is its Section 7.2.7).

Repair channel versus unicast repair. A publisher using this scheme broadcasts repair symbols on the multicast channel (the repair track) rather than relying on unicast retransmission. Receivers covered by the repair flow have no need to drive unicast repair for losses the FEC recovers, which preserves the O(1) sender cost that motivates broadcast FEC. Unicast repair remains a last resort for losses exceeding the repair budget, and Section 11.4 specifies it.

section.t: Item 1 assumes iso-ssbg1-v1, under which one MMTP packet is one source symbol. This document defines no multicast carriage for moq-object-v1 (Section 7.6.6).

A receiver deduplicates the symbols it receives on a multicast QUIC channel as on any other path, within one FEC instance: source symbols by SS_ID and repair symbols by (SS_Start, RS_ID). Section 8.3 states that requirement; states none for application symbols. Section 8.3 also permits combining them with symbols received from other paths.

section.name: Receiver Repair Policy
section.t: This section specifies what a receiver of a multicast or AMT leg does with a base-instance block of a source track that in-band FEC has not recovered by the block's FEC deadline (Section 9). A receiver on a reliable MoQ/QUIC leg relies on transport retransmission (Section 3) and does not need it, and nothing in this section adds a deadline or a timer to such a leg. Multicast and AMT legs carry only mmtp tracks ( Section 5), so this section, which classifies blocks from MMTP fields, concerns tracks under iso-ssbg1-v1.

Every step of this section is keyed on a block's FEC deadline, which exists only when the track's catalog carries a positive interleaveDepthMs (Section 9). On a multicast or AMT leg, this section therefore requires a positive interleaveDepthMs: a receiver of a track whose catalog omits it or sets it to zero MUST disable the block classification and unicast repair of this section for that track. The receiver still decodes in-band FEC from the symbols that arrive (Section 8.3), with open-block state bounded by the local policy of Section 9. Media still missing at its presentation time is lost: the loss of a RAP, or of a data unit that governs one, is handled as for an unrecoverable keyframe-bearing block (Section 11.4.2), and other loss is concealed as in Sections 11.4.3 and 11.4.4.

Every block receives in-band FEC processing. A receiver MUST attempt to recover every block, whatever its class, from the source and repair symbols received on its multicast and AMT paths, together with any it receives on other paths (Section 8.3), up to the block's FEC deadline. Within a consumer that the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2 governs for its blocks (Section 7.4), a symbol of an unlisted track (Section 7.4) enters a decode only as step 2 of Section 7.2.7 allows, which takes none into a decode of a block that two decodes with such symbols' help have left unrecovered; the attempt continues from the symbols the profile admits. The rest of this section governs only a block that is still unrecovered at that deadline: the receiver does not hold all of its SSB_length source symbols (Section 7.4), and decoding from the symbols it holds has not recovered them. Within such a consumer, a source symbol the profile has not admitted, received or recovered, is not held for this purpose (step 2 of Section 7.2.7).

A run of SS_IDs that the receiver lacks and that lies in no block it has delimited belongs to one or more blocks of which it holds no repair packet (Section 7.4). For this section the receiver treats such a run as one block of the instance (within a consumer that the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2 governs for its blocks, Section 7.4, a block only symbols of an unlisted track have delimited being no block the receiver has delimited, and the run one only once a packet the profile has admitted lies above it, step 2 of Section 7.2.7): Section 11.4.1 classifies it from the source packets the receiver holds on either side of it, and its repair is requested by the Group range of Section 7.5, whose response also delimits the blocks it covers.

The policy distinguishes keyframe-bearing blocks, whose loss can stop video decoding until the next Random Access Point (RAP), from other blocks, whose loss damages only frames up to the next RAP. Keyframe-bearing blocks are protected by priority unicast repair and are the only blocks whose loss may stall video. Other blocks are repaired on a best-effort basis and, when repair fails, concealed. Every frame and audio sample a receiver presents MUST be presented at its authored time on the presentation clock shared by its tracks, and a receiver MUST NOT stall video or pause that clock except for a keyframe-bearing block (Section 11.4.2).

section.name: Block Classification
section.t: A base block of a video source track is keyframe-bearing if it carries, or may carry, any part of a RAP: a fragment of a RAP MFU, or of the FT=0 or FT=1 data unit that governs it ( Sections 4.3 and 5.1). The receiver classifies each block when the block reaches its FEC deadline, from two inputs and only from them: in-band evidence in the source packets it holds, and the catalog-authored timing of the track, that is its group structure, one MPU per group of the catalog group duration ( Sections 4.3 and 4.4.2), and its keyframe interval ( Section 4.4.3). The block's SS_Start and SSB_length, once known (Section 7.4), fix which SS_IDs belong to the block, and a positive interleaveDepthMs with reorderToleranceMs fixes the elapsed-time deadline at which the class is taken (Section 9).

The receiver first bounds what the block's missing source symbols can carry. The lower bounding packet is the last source packet it holds, in SS_ID order, before the block's first missing source symbol; the upper bounding packet is the first source packet it holds after the block's last missing source symbol. Either may lie in an adjacent block. Only FEC source symbols count: the AL-FEC signaling object of Section 8 carries no SS_ID and is never a bounding packet. A publisher MUST assign the base SS_IDs of a track's source packets in increasing order along the authored order of Section 4.3, so every data unit the missing symbols can carry lies between the data units of the two bounding packets, those two included.
The block is keyframe-bearing if any of the following holds:

li.t: A source packet the receiver holds from the block sets RAP_flag, carries the 0x8B01 overlay header extension (Section 8.5.1), or is an FT=0 packet, or two source packets it holds from the block carry different MPU sequence numbers.

The two bounding packets carry different MPU sequence numbers, or the lower bounding packet is the FT=0 packet or the first FT=1 packet of its MPU, or belongs to the first FT=2 sample of its MPU. The missing symbols can then carry part of a group-start RAP, or of the metadata that governs it ( Section 4.3).

The catalog carries a usable keyframe interval, and the closed interval between the authored decode times ( Section 5.1) of the samples of the two bounding packets contains an instant a positive whole number of keyframe intervals after the decode time of the first sample of their MPU. Where a bounding packet is an FT=1 packet, its time is the decode time of the first sample it describes. The interval is keyframeIntervalTicks, or keyframeIntervalMs converted to the track timescale where that conversion is exact; an inexact keyframeIntervalMs gives no usable interval.

section.t: The block is non-keyframe-bearing only when none of these holds, the catalog carries a usable keyframe interval, the receiver holds both bounding packets, and it can determine every value item 3 needs. Every other block is of unknown class, and a receiver MUST treat a block of unknown class as keyframe-bearing. In particular:

li.t: A block for which the receiver holds no lower or no upper bounding packet at its FEC deadline is of unknown class, as is one for which it cannot determine a decode time that item 3 needs. So is a block discarded before its FEC deadline under a memory cap (Section 9).

On a video track whose catalog entry carries no usable keyframe interval, the receiver cannot exclude a keyframe after the group start from any span, so every block of the track is keyframe-bearing or of unknown class.

A block's keyframe classification uses its actual source-packet range. A block MAY contain a complete Group, span a Group boundary, or close inside a Group; none of those shapes is inferred from interleaveDepthMs or from the catalog's group duration.

section.t: A receiver MUST NOT classify a block from any input other than those this section names; in particular, the absence of RAP_flag on the packets it holds says nothing about a packet that was lost. A publisher that wants receivers to be able to apply the non-keyframe treatment of Section 11.4.3 publishes an exact keyframe interval, which then binds every keyframe of the track ( Section 4.4.3).

The blocks of a track that the catalog identifies as audio are treated by Section 11.4.4, not classified by this section. A track that the receiver cannot identify from its catalog entry is treated as video.

section.name: Keyframe-Bearing Blocks
section.t: When a keyframe-bearing block is still unrecovered at its FEC deadline, a receiver that holds a MoQ session with a relay serving the block's repair track MUST request on-demand unicast repair for it, with the priority of Section 11.4.5, unless the block lies below a RAP the receiver has already admitted complete (the repair would be moot on completion, below); within a consumer that the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2 governs for its blocks (Section 7.4), a block only symbols of an unlisted track (Section 7.4) have delimited reaches no deadline and is never requested, the SS_IDs it covers that the receiver lacks being runs of this section (step 2 of Section 7.2.7). The request is a FETCH , over QUIC, of the block's repair-track group, whose Group ID is the block's extended SS_Start, or, for a run that the receiver has not delimited, of the Group range that Section 7.5 derives from a lost SS_ID x of the run. The receiver sends it on layer 0, and on further layers in layer order where it needs more symbols than layer 0 carries (Sections 6.3.2 and 6.3.5). Section 7.5 gives the LOCATION_FILTER of either form, and the receiver establishes the wrap epoch as Section 7.5 specifies, for instance by a TRACK_STATUS request when it has received no repair-track Group ID over MoQ. The FETCH of a single group MAY be limited to the object range that covers the block's shortfall. The repair symbols it returns are deduplicated against the symbols already held by (SS_Start, RS_ID) (Section 8.3) and fed to the same decoder; their SS_Start and SSB_length also delimit a block the receiver had not delimited (Section 7.4). The receiver MUST NOT delay this request behind any non-keyframe or audio repair; Section 11.4.6 covers its interplay with a keyframe overlay. A FETCH completes or fails by MoQ Transport events, its last object or an error; a receiver MUST NOT declare it failed on a locally chosen timeout.

Only a keyframe-bearing block may stall video. While its unicast repair is outstanding, the receiver MAY hold video presentation for it. The block is unrecoverable when its unicast repair fails or completes without recovering it, or when the receiver holds no MoQ session through which to request it (for example a receiver that consumes an MMTP stream without a MoQ session, Section 1.1). If the data of an unrecoverable block that the receiver could not recover includes, or may include, any part of a RAP (Section 11.4.1), the receiver treats the track as discontinuous, MAY stall video, and does not resume video before the next RAP ( Section 6.1, step 6). Otherwise, as when it holds or has recovered every part of the block's RAPs (including through a keyframe overlay, Section 11.4.6), it conceals the block's remaining loss as for a non-keyframe block (Section 11.4.3).

If the next RAP arrives complete before a keyframe repair completes, the repair is moot: the receiver resumes from that RAP and SHOULD cancel the FETCH; a block that reaches its deadline already below such a RAP is not requested at all.

section.name: Other Video Blocks
section.t: For a non-keyframe-bearing block of a video track, in-band FEC remains the primary repair. A receiver MAY also request unicast repair for it, in the form of Section 11.4.2, but only on the terms of Section 11.4.5: never ahead of or concurrently with keyframe repair, and only within the budget that keyframe repair leaves unspent.

When such a block is unrecovered -- at its FEC deadline without unicast repair, or when its unicast repair has not completed by the presentation time of the first media it would repair -- the receiver MUST NOT stall. It conceals the affected frames, and every frame that depends on them, until the next RAP, and keeps presentation and audio/video synchronization running:

li.t: Concealment fills the presentation interval of the frames it replaces and ends at the authored presentation time of the next frame the receiver presents. The receiver MUST NOT drop later frames to absorb the loss. It derives no timing for the frames it replaces ( Section 5.1).

The concealment method is an implementation choice: for example holding or replaying the last presented frame, or presenting decoder output in which missing reference data is filled (commonly visible as a solid or green fill). The receiver MUST NOT submit to the decoder a sample that the packaging's reassembly rules have invalidated ( Section 5.2).
The next RAP ends concealment, and the receiver resumes normal decoding from it.

section.name: Audio Blocks
section.t: In-band FEC applies to the blocks of an audio track as to every block, and a receiver MAY request unicast repair for an audio block on the same best-effort terms as for a non-keyframe video block (Section 11.4.5). RAP_flag on an audio packet does not make its block keyframe-bearing; that class applies to video tracks only.

When an audio block is unrecovered, the receiver MUST conceal the lost audio, for example with silence or packet-loss concealment, from the end of the last audio it presented to the authored presentation time of the next audio it presents, and MUST keep the audio clock advancing through the loss. It MUST NOT stall audio presentation waiting for a repair that has not completed by the presentation time of the lost audio.

section.name: Unicast Repair Budget and Priority
section.t: A receiver's unicast repair budget is derived from the catalog, not from a receiver-local rate or byte constant. It is kept per MoQ session and counted in bytes of repair symbol data, a repair symbol of a track counting as that track's symbolSize T (Section 5.1).

li.t: Each block that Section 11.4.1 treats as keyframe-bearing, including a block of unknown class, credits the budget with P_t x T bytes when it reaches its FEC deadline, where P_t is the total repair count of its base instance (Section 6.4.1) and T is its track's symbolSize.
A credit expires when the next keyframe-bearing block of the same source track reaches its FEC deadline, so unspent budget never accumulates beyond one block's credit per source track.

Every unicast repair FETCH debits the budget with the repair symbol bytes it requests. A FETCH of a Group range (Section 7.5) requests every Group that starts in the range, a number the receiver learns only from the response, and is debited with the repair symbol bytes of every Group it returns.

A receiver does not withhold a keyframe-bearing block's repair for lack of credit. For a block that it has delimited, it requests at most one repair-track Group per base repair layer, that is at most the P_t x T bytes that the block itself credits. For a run of blocks that it has not delimited, it issues the one Group range FETCH of Section 7.5 per base repair layer. Each Group that FETCH returns is the repair of one block of the run, and every block holds at least one SS_ID of a range that spans at most K SS_IDs (Section 7.5), so these FETCHes cost at most K x P_t x T bytes in all, which can exceed the credit. A debit that exceeds the remaining credit exhausts it: the budget never falls below zero, and no deficit carries over to a later credit. A receiver MUST NOT have more than one repair FETCH outstanding for the same block and repair layer.

Non-keyframe and audio repair MAY spend only unexpired credit that keyframe-bearing blocks left unspent, and a receiver MUST NOT issue a non-keyframe or audio repair FETCH that the remaining credit does not cover. Because the cost of a Group range FETCH is not known before it is issued, a receiver MUST NOT request non-keyframe or audio repair by a Group range.

A receiver MUST NOT issue a non-keyframe or audio repair FETCH while a keyframe repair FETCH is outstanding on the same session, and SHOULD cancel its outstanding non-keyframe and audio repair FETCHes when it requests the repair of a keyframe-bearing block that reaches its FEC deadline unrecovered; a block whose repair Section 11.4.2 does not request cancels nothing.

section.t: Priorities follow the ranges of Section 10. A keyframe repair FETCH MUST carry a SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY ( Section 9.20.7) in the Source Media range, numerically at most 191. It MUST also be numerically no greater than the SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY of the receiver's subscription to the source track, where the receiver holds one on the session, and numerically lower than the SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY of every repair-track subscription that the receiver holds on the session. Subscriber priority is compared first ( Section 5.1.2), so the FETCH is then delivered ahead of the receiver's repair tracks and is not shed with repair data under congestion. A non-keyframe or audio repair FETCH MUST carry a priority numerically no lower than that of the repair track it fetches, and so at least 192, so that it is shed first.

section.name: Relationship to the Keyframe Overlay
section.t: The keyframe overlay of Section 6.4 and this policy are complementary. The overlay is publisher-side and proactive: it protects RAP fragments across a block of its own, needs no return path, and so also serves sessionless receivers. This policy is receiver-side and reactive: it spends unicast repair only on keyframe-bearing blocks that in-band FEC actually failed to recover, and it needs a MoQ session. A receiver that holds both:

li.t: classifies blocks by Section 11.4.1 whether or not it holds the overlay;
ends its wait for a RAP with whichever of base decoding, overlay decoding, or unicast repair supplies the RAP's fragments first; and

having recovered a block's RAP MFU fragments through the overlay, and holding the FT=0 and FT=1 data units that govern them, conceals the rest of that block's loss as for a non-keyframe block (Section 11.4.3) and SHOULD cancel any outstanding keyframe repair FETCH for it. The overlay covers only packets that set RAP_flag (Section 6.4.2), so it does not by itself recover a lost FT=0 or FT=1 data unit.

section.name: ATSC 3.0 Compatibility
section.t: This specification is designed for interoperability with the Application-Layer FEC of ATSC A/331 MMTP sessions. applies AL-FEC to an MMTP session, when it applies it at all, through the AL-FEC framework of Annex C and requires no FEC code of its own (its Section 8.1.2.5): the framework carries whichever code the AL-FEC message names by its code point. The codes are this document's to specify, and it specifies two, "reed-solomon" (code point 1, mandatory to implement) and "raptorq" (code point 3, OPTIONAL) (Sections 4.1 and 4.3); Section 8.3 gives the AL-FEC message a publisher sends for a track of either, and an MMTP session whose AL-FEC message names any other code is outside this document until the registry of Section 15.2 lists that code. A publisher that ingests an A/331 MMTP session takes the FEC parameters of its tracks from that message and the asset locations of the MP table ( Section 12.2), and a receiver that consumes the session without the catalog takes them from the message alone, holding the one repair flow as layer 0 under the block total the message bounds, which stands for its O_0 + P_0 in the check of Section 6.3.9, applied to layer 0 by its anchored clause alone, so that a packet of the flow generated under the previous total, which the message can precede ( Section 8.3), fails it closed on nothing. An MMTP session carries no OTI: the derived OTI of Section 4.2 fixes N = 1, and sub-blocks are never used (Section 7.3). ROUTE delivery, whose repair protocol (Annex A.4 of ) is RaptorQ-based, is outside the scope of this document.

section.name: Interaction with CMAF Packaging
section.t: This section is informative.
A track carrying CMAF content can be protected in two ways.

Under moq-object-v1 (Section 7.6), a repair track protects a cmaf track directly. Each object of the cmaf track holds one or more CMAF chunks ( Section 3.3) and forms one Protected Object Unit, and each Group begins with an object that contains a Stream Access Point (SAP) ( Section 3.4):

Alternatively, the publisher carries the media as an mmtp track under iso-ssbg1-v1, where an MPU corresponds to a CMAF Fragment (see ). Such a track is also how CMAF content reaches multicast, because a multicast endpoint carries only mmtp tracks ( Section 4.1). The cmaf track and its mmtp rendition are separate FEC instances, and symbols of one never repair the other.

A publisher can choose a segment duration equal to interleaveDepthMs and close blocks at segment boundaries, so that a segment holds one chosen block's source symbols and a CDN relay can perform FEC recovery at the segment level before forwarding to FEC-unaware HLS/DASH clients. The boundary is an explicit publisher choice; the duration alone does not create or identify a block.

section.name: FEC Does Not Provide Confidentiality
section.t: FEC repair symbols are derived from source data. If source data is encrypted, repair symbols will also be encrypted by virtue of operating on ciphertext. However, FEC itself provides no confidentiality guarantees.

section.name: Repair Symbol Manipulation
section.t: An attacker who can modify repair symbols could cause receivers to reconstruct incorrect source data. Integrity protection of repair tracks is RECOMMENDED, using the same mechanisms as source tracks (e.g., QUIC packet protection).

section.name: Amplification
section.t: FEC repair symbols represent additional bandwidth. Publishers MUST NOT generate excessive repair symbols that could be used for bandwidth amplification attacks. The repair overhead (P/K) SHOULD be limited to reasonable values (e.g., <= 50%). The bound applies per FEC instance (Section 6.4.1), and for the base instance to P_0/K, the repair that a receiver gets by default: further repair layers are added on demand (Sections 6.3.5 and 6.3.6), and the next paragraph covers them.

Layering changes the shape of the amplification exposure, because the attacker's lever is now which layers a victim can be made to receive rather than only whether it receives repair at all. Each layer i adds P_i x T bytes per source block, so a receiver induced to hold more layers receives proportionally more repair traffic. Deployments SHOULD bound the number of layers any single receiver may hold, and SHOULD apply the same join authorization to repair-layer endpoints as to media endpoints; a repair-only endpoint (Section 6.3.6) is not less sensitive than a media one merely because it carries no media.

A receiver MUST NOT be made to receive a repair layer it did not join. A publisher or relay MUST NOT push a repair-layer endpoint to a receiver that has not joined it, and MUST NOT add a layer to an endpoint a receiver has already joined as a way of raising that receiver's protection.

section.name: Multicast FEC Security
section.t: When FEC is used over multicast (SSM/AMT), which carries only mmtp tracks under iso-ssbg1-v1 ( Section 4.1), additional considerations apply:

li.t: No QUIC Protection: Multicast UDP has neither the confidentiality nor the integrity of QUIC. A publisher that needs confidentiality SHOULD encrypt the media samples, for example with Common Encryption and its 'cbcs' scheme, as Section 13 describes for mmtp tracks. All receivers of the flow share the content keys, which reach each receiver over its unicast MoQ session or from a Digital Rights Management (DRM) system. Sample encryption leaves the MMTP headers and the Source FEC Payload ID in the clear and leaves every packet identical across paths, so FEC encodes the ciphertext (Section 14.1) and symbols still combine across paths (Section 8.3). Encrypting each MoQ object payload instead, as MoQ Secure Objects does, would make the MoQ copy of a packet differ from its multicast copy. A keying handshake per receiver, such as DTLS-SRTP, needs a return path and cannot key a one-to-many flow. A key that every receiver holds does not authenticate the publisher; item 3 covers authentication.

Repair Injection: Attackers could inject malicious repair symbols on multicast networks. Receivers SHOULD verify FEC block consistency by checking that decoded data matches expected patterns (e.g., valid media container structure).

Source Authentication: SSM limits which sources reach a receiver ( Section 7.1), and version 2 of the bc-provenance profile ( Section 7.2) authenticates the datagrams themselves, repair symbols included, with a digest that covers the whole UDP payload, the Source FEC Payload ID included (Section 8.5).

Block Integrity: Receivers MAY implement block-level checksums to detect corrupted recovery. A block whose decoded source data fails such a check, or, within a consumer that the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2 governs for its blocks (Section 7.4), whose recovered packets step 2 of its Section 7.2.7 does not admit, is unrecovered: Section 11.4 governs it from its FEC deadline, and the receiver requests unicast repair for it only as that section directs, never by the multicast-to-unicast failover of , which replaces the multicast path.

Repair Policy Inputs: The in-band evidence that Section 11.4.1 classifies blocks from, and the SSB_length by which Section 7.4 completes a short block, are unauthenticated on bare multicast. An injected packet that marks a block keyframe-bearing costs at most the unicast repair that block's own credit covers (Section 11.4.5). An injected source packet inside a block's gap can instead narrow the bounds of Section 11.4.1 until a keyframe-bearing block is classified otherwise, and an injected repair packet carrying a false SS_Start or SSB_length, accepted before the genuine ones, can mis-delimit a block, mark it complete early, or cause its genuine repair packets to be discarded as inconsistent (Section 7.4). Deployments exposed to injection SHOULD authenticate source and repair packets with an integrity mechanism whose coverage includes the complete packet, the Source FEC Payload ID and the Repair FEC Payload ID included (Section 8.5). Version 2 of the bc-provenance profile ( Section 7.2) is such a mechanism: its digest covers the whole UDP payload of source and repair packets, both Payload IDs included.

section.name: ATSC 3.0 Signed Region (A3SA) Considerations
section.t: Under iso-ssbg1-v1, the Source FEC Payload ID falls outside the A3SA signed region, and neither nor provides a carriage of the SS_ID inside it (Section 8.5). An attacker who can modify it without detection could redirect source symbols to incorrect FEC blocks, causing recovery failures or corrupted output. A receiver that requires authenticated FEC block assignment therefore treats the trailer as Section 8.5 requires. On multicast networks without A3SA verification, receivers SHOULD cross-check the SS_ID against the MMTP packet_sequence_number to detect obvious tampering (e.g., an SS_ID that advances further than the packet_sequence_number of the same packet_id, whereas SS_ID advances by one per FEC source packet, Section 8.3).

section.name: Object Block Profile Considerations
section.t: Under moq-object-v1 a receiver takes the lengths of a rebuilt object from decoded bytes (Section 7.6.4). A corrupt decode, from damaged or injected repair symbols, can put any value there. A receiver MUST NOT read, copy or allocate beyond the end of the run it walks on the strength of the Immutable Properties Length or the Payload Length. The checks of Section 7.6.4 discard a run whose units do not tile it exactly or whose padding is not zero. They detect many corrupt decodes, but not all.

A block of this profile holds K x T bytes of source data at most, and no unit is longer (Section 7.6.2), so sourceSymbols and symbolSize bound the memory one open block needs. A receiver MAY decline FEC for a track whose K x T exceeds its local limits, and it bounds the number of open blocks by the policy of Section 9.

A unit includes the object's Immutable Properties exactly as serialized. A relay that alters them, which Section 10.7 forbids, changes the unit a receiver builds from the object, and silently corrupts the recovery of the other objects of its block. A relay that adds, changes or removes mutable Properties does not affect FEC, because they are not in the unit.

MoQ Secure Objects authenticates the Group ID, Object ID, Publisher Priority and serialized Immutable Properties of an object, along with its payload ( Section 3.5). The unit carries all of these except the Publisher Priority, which Section 7.6.5 asks publishers to make known. A receiver can then verify a rebuilt object as it verifies a received one, and discards one that fails. With the FEC Source Info Property inside Immutable Properties, the same verification authenticates the SS_ID of each object it accepts.

section.name: Reed-Solomon Considerations
section.t: The catalog bounds the cost of reed-solomon decoding. A block has at most 255 source and repair symbols (Section 4.5), so the number of source symbols a receiver recovers in it, E, is at most min(SSB_length, RSB_length), which is at most 127. The receiver inverts one E x E matrix per block and performs about E x SSB_length x T multiplications in GF(2^8) to form and apply the result (Section 4.4). One open block holds at most 255 x T bytes of symbols.

The code provides no integrity protection, as RaptorQ provides none (Section 14.2). A decoder that is given a corrupted or injected symbol yields wrong source symbols and reports no error, and when it decodes from exactly SSB_length symbols the code itself cannot reveal the error. The checks of Sections 7.3 and 7.6.4 reject some wrong results. A receiver that holds more than SSB_length symbols of a block can also re-encode the recovered block and compare the result with the symbols it did not use: a mismatch shows that some symbol it holds is not what the publisher encoded.

section.name: MoQ Registrations
section.t: This document requests one registration in the "MOQ Properties" registry of (Section 8.4 of that document):

The type is odd, so under the key-value parity rule of the Property is length-prefixed and byte-valued (Section 5.3). The scope is Object: FEC Source Info describes the individual object it tags, and carries no track-wide meaning.

0x11 lies in the range 0x00 to 0x77, for which states a registration policy of Standards Action or IESG Approval. That policy is not reachable by an individual draft, so this document asks for 0x11 as a provisional registration in the table maintains for other active drafts in the MoQ working group, on the same terms as the existing entries for draft-ietf-moq-loc and draft-ietf-moq-secure-objects. That ask is contingent on this document being adopted. If 0x11 is not available on those terms, an odd value in the range 0x80 to 0x37FF, whose policy is Specification Required, is obtainable by this document on its own. It costs at most one additional byte per tagged object, because Property types are delta-coded ( Section 8.3) and the extra byte appears only when the encoded Delta Type exceeds 127. It changes nothing else in this specification.

The even value 0x10, used by deployed implementations for this purpose, is deliberately not requested, and this document could not reserve it in any case: already lists 0x10 as the TIMESTAMP Object Property of draft-ietf-moq-loc, at Object scope in the same Property Type space. Section 5.3 gives the resulting collision and its consequences.

This document requests no registration in any MoQ message type registry. FEC signaling uses no MoQ control message (Section 5.2); no document in this suite requests a control-message codepoint. The header extension type 0x8B01 of Section 8.5.1 is an MMTP value, not a MoQ one; Clause 9.2.3 defines no registry of MMTP header extension types, so its use requires no IANA action.

section.name: FEC Algorithm Registry
section.t: This document requests creation of a "MoQ FEC Algorithms" registry, in a new "Media over QUIC (MoQ) Forward Error Correction" registry group, with the following initial values:

The Identifier is the string that the catalog fec.algorithm field carries (Section 5.1). The Value is a one-byte code for the same algorithm; no message or field that this document defines carries it. New registrations require Specification Required policy ( Section 4.6). A registration supplies an unassigned Value, an Identifier that no other entry uses, the algorithm's name, and a reference to its specification. The designated expert checks that the specification gives the algorithm's symbol construction, the derivation of its decoder parameters from the catalog and the Repair FEC Payload ID, and the semantics of its repair objects (Section 4.3), and that it states whether the algorithm admits repair layers and the keyframe overlay (Section 6.3.3).

This document specifies "None" (0x00), RaptorQ (0x01) and Reed-Solomon (0x02) for interoperation. Other registered values are extension points whose interoperable use requires their own specifications (Section 4.3).

section.name: Catalog Packaging Value
section.t: This document defines the catalog packaging value "fec-repair" (Section 5.1) for repair tracks, extending the allowed packaging values of the MOQT Streaming Format Section 5.2.4. If a registry of packaging values is established for that format, this document requests registration of:

tr.td: Repair objects protecting a source track

section.name: FEC Block Profile Registry
section.t: This document requests creation of a "MoQ FEC Block Profiles" registry, in the registry group of Section 15.2, with the following initial values:

The Block Profile is the string that the catalog fec.blockProfile field carries (Section 5.1). New registrations require Specification Required policy ( Section 4.6). A registration supplies a Block Profile string that no other entry uses, the source track packaging values that it admits, and a reference to its specification. The designated expert checks that the specification fixes what Section 5.1 requires of a block profile: how source symbols are formed from a source packet or a source object, how many source symbols a block holds, how a block and the source symbols in it are identified, and how those identifiers wrap.

section.name: Catalog-Driven FEC
section.t: The subscriber learns the complete FEC configuration from the track's catalog entry before subscribing:
section.artwork: Publisher Subscriber | | | (catalog obtained by SUBSCRIBE with | | request_id=0; fec field read) | | | | SUBSCRIBE(request_id=2, track=video, | | LOCATION_FILTER=0x05 (Next Object), | | FILL_PARAMETERS(LOCATION_FILTER= | | 0x01, StartGroup=1)) | |<-----------------------------------------| | | | SUBSCRIBE_OK(LARGEST_OBJECT={G, n}) | |----------------------------------------->| | | | SUBSCRIBE(request_id=4, | | track=video/repair, | | LOCATION_FILTER=0x05 (Next Object)) | |<-----------------------------------------| | | | SUBSCRIBE_OK | |----------------------------------------->| | | | [Fill fetch stream: source objects | | {G, 0} to {G, n}] | |----------------------------------------->| | | | [Source objects from {G, n+1} on] | |----------------------------------------->| | | | [Repair objects, group=ext(SS_Start), | | obj=0..7] | |----------------------------------------->| | |
section.t: Each SUBSCRIBE carries a Request ID ( Section 6.4.2.1). A client uses even Request IDs, starting at 0 and rising by 2 per request, so the catalog SUBSCRIBE ( Section 5) takes 0 and the source and repair SUBSCRIBEs take 2 and 4. Each response travels on the bidirectional stream of its request, so SUBSCRIBE_OK carries no Request ID. The source subscription joins at the start of the current Group G ( Section 3.5; Section 6.1). Its Next Object filter starts subscription delivery at {G, n+1}, where {G, n} is the Largest Object that SUBSCRIBE_OK reports, and its fill range, from {G, 0} to that Largest Object, arrives on a fill fetch stream. The repair subscription starts at the Next Object; repair objects published before it can be requested by FETCH (Section 7.5).

In this flow the track is mmtp-packaged with a one-second group duration (one MPU per MoQ Group, Section 4.3). That group duration describes the MoQ grouping; it does not derive an FEC block. For example, if the first block starts at SS_ID 0 and is full, its repair Group is its extended SS_Start, 0 (Section 7.5), the next block starts at SS_ID 32, and its repair Group is 32. A publisher MAY choose shorter blocks inside a Group or a block that crosses the Group boundary; each repair packet carries the actual SSB_length. The subscriber's decoder configuration is derived from the catalog fields and each block's SSB_length (Section 4.2): for a full block (SSB_length = K = 32), Transfer Length F = SSB_length x T = 32 x 1312 = 41,984 bytes, Symbol Size T = 1312, Z = 1, N = 1, Al = 8. No in-session message is required, and this track carries no AL-FEC signaling object ( Section 8).
A loc or cmaf track under moq-object-v1 follows the same flow. Its source objects carry the FEC Source Info Property as Section 7.6.2 specifies, and its repair objects are those of Section 7.6.3.

section.name: Catalog Example
section.t: Complete catalog with FEC and multicast configuration:

Parameter consistency: both tracks use one-second MMTP groups (one MPU per MoQ Group), and each has a 1000 ms source/repair send-span budget. The group duration does not determine the FEC partition. A worked capacity check must include the MMTP and MPU-mode headers, not only the media bitrate. With no MMTP header extension, a timed FT=2 packet has the following media capacity, depending on whether it starts a data unit ( Section 5.2):
section.artwork: FI=0 or FI=1: T - 2 (length) - 12 (MMTP) - 8 (MPU) - 14 (DU) = T - 36 FI=2 or FI=3: T - 2 (length) - 12 (MMTP) - 8 (MPU) = T - 22
section.t: The source packet also carries a 4-byte Source FEC Payload ID on the wire, outside the protected packet and therefore outside these symbol budgets. FT=0/FT=1 metadata consumes source packets but does not carry sample bytes, and any MMTP extension consumes additional space. Every protected MMTP packet still MUST fit within T - 2. Using the larger continuation capacity gives a media ceiling, not a packetization plan:

ul.li: Video: 4,990,000 bit/s x 1.0 s / 8 = 623,750 bytes of media per one-second group. K x (T - 22) = 625 x 978 = 611,250 bytes is an upper bound on the media capacity of one full block. The media therefore needs at least ceil(623,750 / 978) = 638 source packets and at least two K=625 blocks; MMTP metadata, fragmentation, and authored packet boundaries can require more. Repair overhead is P / K = 125 / 625 = 20%.

Audio: 128,000 bit/s x 1.0 s / 8 = 16,000 bytes of media per group; the upper-bound capacity of one full block is K x (T - 22) = 32 x 490 = 15,680 bytes. The media therefore needs at least ceil(16,000 / 490) = 33 source packets and at least two K=32 blocks; packetization and metadata can require more. Repair overhead is P / K = 8 / 32 = 25%.

section.t: The publisher MUST choose the actual source-packet count and block boundaries so that every packet, including FT=0 and FT=1 metadata, fits the selected symbol size and every block's repair fields describe the actual (SS_Start, SSB_length) partition. These calculations are capacity examples, not a rule that one FEC block equals one Group.

The catalog envelope is the MSF root ( Section 5.1); track entries carry the flat base track fields of Section 5.2 (codec, width, samplerate, ...) alongside the fec object this document defines, and inherit the namespace of the catalog track ( Section 5.2.2). The multicast field uses the multicast endpoint format defined in Section 4.1: a one-element endpoints array. Per Sections 4.1 and 5, a multicast endpoint lists only mmtp tracks and their repair tracks, and a loc or cmaf track reaches multicast through an mmtp rendition track. Each track listed on the endpoint carries a packetId that routes its MMTP packets on the multicast UDP path. Section 7.6.7 gives a loc track under moq-object-v1, whose capacity is counted in Protected Object Units rather than MMTP packets.

section.name: Changes Since draft-ramadan-moq-fec-00
section.t: This appendix is informative and is to be removed before publication as an RFC.

ul.li: Added Marc E. Fiuczynski as an author.

Removed Section 5.4 (Relay Extensibility Requirements) and its item in the Introduction. Its first rule contradicted Section 9, under which an unknown control message type closes the session, and its second rule restated Section 8.4 of that document without the caching requirement and the Mandatory Track Property exception. Section 5.3 now cites Section 8.4 for relay handling of Properties that a relay does not support. Section 5.4 was the last subsection of Section 5, so no section is renumbered.
Section 3: delivery on QUIC streams is reliable only until a delivery timeout or a stream reset abandons an object.
Section 5.1: removed the note about an unpublished earlier revision of the iso-ssbg1-v1 profile.
Section 5.1: repairTrack is a Track Name in the source track's Track Namespace.

Section 5.1.1: priority is the Publisher Priority of the repair track's objects, and a subscriber should not subscribe to a repair track with a numerically lower subscriber priority than its source subscription. Section 10 refers to this.
Sections 5.3 and 15.1: the registry is "MOQ Properties". A fallback type in 0x80 to 0x37FF costs at most one extra byte per object, because Property types are delta-coded.

Section 6.1: a repair track is in its source track's Track Namespace. The layer-0 Track Name formed by appending "/repair" to the source Track Name is a convention, replacing the required namespace tuple of -00, and the examples show namespace and name separately.
Section 6.3: the rule against listing a repair track without its source binds an entity that republishes a catalog subset, since relays do not parse catalogs.

Section 7.5: MoQ Transport Group IDs reach 2^64 - 1, and this document uses [0, 2^62) on purpose. LARGEST_OBJECT is cited as Section 9.20.17, "Largest Location" is now "Largest Object", and the repair FETCH states its LOCATION_FILTER encoding, the object range of type 0x04 included. The section notes the departure from the Group numbering of Section 6.1 and allows PRIOR_GROUP_ID_GAP on repair objects. A publisher that starts a new source encoding, including after a restart that loses its FEC state, publishes it under new Full Track Names, so that repair Group IDs never repeat under one name.

Section 11.3: rewrote the description of : channel acknowledgments are MC_ACK frames, Section 8 of that document recommends FEC repair packets, and integrity rests on MC_INTEGRITY hashes. Deduplication by FEC coordinates is this document's requirement. The reference is now informative, and so is the subsection, which uses no BCP 14 keywords.
Section 11.4.2: "standalone FETCH" is now FETCH, and the section refers to Section 7.5 for the LOCATION_FILTER of the request.
Section 14.4: confidentiality on multicast uses Common Encryption of the media samples instead of DTLS-SRTP, and source authentication cites Sections 7.1 and 7.2.
Appendix A.1: requests carry Request IDs, starting at 0 for the catalog SUBSCRIBE, and the source subscription joins with a Next Object filter and FILL_PARAMETERS.

New Section 7.6: the block profile moq-object-v1 protects tracks packaged as loc or cmaf. A source object's Protected Object Unit (Group ID, Object ID, Immutable Properties and payload, with fixed-width lengths) spans s(o) zero-padded source symbols, and its FEC Source Info Property carries the SS_ID of the first one. Blocks hold whole units, and repair objects carry no MMTP header. The section specifies the receiver's recovery walk and checks, requires loc publishers to carry presentation Properties inside Immutable Properties, asks publishers that use Secure Objects to give every object the track's default Publisher Priority, states the profile's applicability, and works an example.

Abstract and Section 1: the document defines two block profiles, and the ATSC 3.0 and ARIB compatibility statement concerns the MMTP profile. Section 1 promises an ATSC 3.0 MMTP compatibility statement only, and points to for ARIB STD-B60 carriage.
Section 2: the Repair Track, Source Block, Source Symbol, SS_ID, Interleave Depth, Keyframe Overlay and Block Profile definitions cover both profiles, and Protected Object Unit is defined.
Section 4.2: the derived OTI refers to the source symbol construction of the track's block profile.

Section 5.1: blockProfile defines moq-object-v1 next to iso-ssbg1-v1, and each value names the packaging values it admits. A receiver does not apply FEC under a profile that does not admit the track's packaging. sourceSymbols counts symbols, symbolSize states the object profile's capacity, and a zero interleaveDepthMs under moq-object-v1 equals an absent field.
Section 5.1.1 and Section 6.3.4, rule 1: depends names a track whose blockProfile admits its packaging, instead of requiring mmtp.
Section 5.1.1 and Section 6.3.4, rule 10: a keyframe overlay is defined only under iso-ssbg1-v1, and a catalog that declares one for a track under moq-object-v1 fails closed. Section 6.4 states why.
Section 5.1.1: an overlay's sourceSymbols MUST be >= 1, a floor that -00 did not state. Section 6.3.4, rule 13 makes it a catalog rule a receiver fails closed on.
Section 5.2: loc and cmaf tracks have no in-band FEC signaling.

Section 5.3: the FEC Source Info Property carries the SS_ID of an object's first source symbol under moq-object-v1, where it is the only SS_ID carrier, and the recoverable length rule covers both profiles.
Sections 6.3, 6.3.6, 7.3, 8.5, 11.4, 14.4 and 14.5: text that depends on MMTP is scoped to iso-ssbg1-v1.
Section 7.1: the MMTP repair packet form applies under iso-ssbg1-v1, and the Repair FEC Payload ID fields apply under both profiles.
Sections 6.3.1, 7.4, 7.5, 8 and 8.3: block, FETCH and source symbol location rules speak of source symbols and objects, not only packets, and Section 8.3 scopes cross-path combining per profile.
Sections 8.4 and 9: encoder constraints, the zero interleaveDepthMs and the conformance cases are stated per profile.
Sections 11.1, 11.2 and 11.3: multicast carries mmtp tracks only, and a loc or cmaf track reaches it through an mmtp rendition track.
Section 13: rewritten. A cmaf track can be protected directly under moq-object-v1, or carried as an mmtp track, which is also its route to multicast.
New Section 14.6: security considerations for moq-object-v1: length validation, padding checks, memory bounds, relay tampering and Secure Objects.
Appendices A.1 and B: notes on loc tracks and on multicast carriage.
References: added as normative and as informative.

New Sections 4.4 and 4.5: "reed-solomon" (0x02) is fully specified. It is the systematic Cauchy Reed-Solomon code over GF(2^8) of Clause 6 (MMT FEC code point 1), restated with its field, matrix, encoding, short blocks and decoding. Its parameters come from the catalog and the Repair FEC Payload ID, with no OTI. A repair packet whose SSB_length + RSB_length exceeds 255, or whose RS_ID is not below RSB_length, is discarded, except that, on a packet of the own track of a held layer above 0 or on a block to which the fail-closed check of Section 6.3.9 applies, that check takes precedence. Where the restatement and differ, the ISO text governs.

Abstract, Sections 1, 4 and 5.1: the document fully specifies two schemes. Reed-Solomon is now the mandatory-to-implement scheme; RaptorQ, mandatory in -00, is optional (Section 4.3). symbolSize need not be a multiple of 8 under Reed-Solomon, is at least 1 under every profile and at least 14 under iso-ssbg1-v1, and Section 4.5 gives a catalog example.
Section 4.1: both codes are systematic and correspond to the code points 3 and 1. The RaptorQ entry states its decoding overhead.

Section 4.3: retitled "Algorithm Requirements" (it was "Other FEC Algorithms"). It gives the rationale for Reed-Solomon as the mandatory scheme and for keeping RaptorQ: block size. It states that the MMT AL-FEC framework and require no FEC code for an MMTP session, so this document specifies the codes.
Sections 2, 3 and 5.2: definitions and decoder configuration cover both codes.
Section 5.1.2: the worked catalog's overlay is valid only under RaptorQ.
Section 6.3.2: the decoding overhead depends on the algorithm and is zero under Reed-Solomon, and layers combine under either code.

Section 6.3.3: retitled "Algorithms That Admit Layers" (it was "Why RaptorQ Only"), and its rationale is corrected. The -00 text said that a Reed-Solomon code fixes n = K + P at encoding time, so that its symbols for one P are not valid for another. That holds only for the generator-polynomial form. In a systematic construction whose repair columns are fixed by the symbol's index, as in (by SSB_length and RS_ID together) and in the Cauchy construction of Section 4.4 (by RS_ID alone), a repair symbol does not depend on P. The section states conditions (a) to (d) under which an algorithm admits repair layers and the overlay, and the Reed-Solomon code meets them, with K + totalP at most 255.

Section 6.3.4: rule 7 admits reed-solomon, new rule 12 bounds K + totalP by 255 for each Reed-Solomon FEC instance, and new rule 13 makes the range rules of Sections 5.1 and 5.1.1 (sourceSymbols at least 1, repairSymbols at least 1 when a repair track is published and on each repair track where declared, an overlay's sourceSymbols at least 1, now stated in Section 5.1.1, symbolSize at least 1 and, under iso-ssbg1-v1, at least 14, and a multiple of 8 under raptorq) catalog rules a receiver fails closed on.
Sections 6.3.9 and 6.4.1: a layer append, and a keyframe overlay, stay within rule 12 under Reed-Solomon. Section 6.4.1 gives a valid Reed-Solomon overlay.

Section 7.1: under Reed-Solomon RS_ID is the column of A. The encoder rule now names the actual hazard: a layer's symbols must be the block's symbols at the RS_IDs they carry, not a separate encoding relabeled from O_i.
Sections 7.2 and 7.4: Reed-Solomon repair symbols, short blocks, recovery condition and packet checks.
Sections 7.6.2 and 7.6.7: Reed-Solomon limits the largest protected object, and the example is valid only under RaptorQ.
Section 9: the recovery condition follows the track's algorithm.

Section 12: ATSC 3.0 compatibility is MMTP only. The ROUTE mapping of A/331 AL-FEC of -00 (the S-TSID fecOTI, RepairFlow and overhead rules) and the sub-block guidance are removed, and the section states that requires no particular code for an MMTP session and that the codes are this document's to specify.
New Section 14.7: Reed-Solomon decoding cost and the absence of integrity protection.
Section 15.2: the Reed-Solomon entry references Clause 6 and Section 4.4, and the code is specified for interoperation.
New Appendix C: Reed-Solomon test vectors. The appendix of changes becomes Appendix D.
References: added as normative.
Section 5.3: a 0x10-tagged FEC object can desynchronize the parse into a session closure, a malformed track or silently wrong values, and not always into a closure. FEC Source Info is single-valued.
Section 6.3.4: an undeclared layer-0 priority binds the publisher to Publisher Priority 240 (rule 3), and the 56403 bound applies under raptorq only (rule 6).

Sections 6.3.8, 6.3.9 and 7.1: RSB_length is the total repair count when a block's repair symbols are generated, so it rises when a layer is appended, and the repair packets of a block generated before an append carry the previous total, below the O_i + P_i of the appended layer, and can reach a receiver that joined the layer after the catalog that lists it. The fail-closed check of Section 6.3.9 therefore applies, for a held layer above 0, to a packet of that layer's own track, whose symbol was generated under a total at or above its O_i + P_i, and for every held layer to a block at or after, in the serial order of Section 7.5, one that carried at least that layer's O_i + P_i; layer 0, whose coordinates depend on no published count, has no clause of its own track, which lets a catalog, or the message held in its place, give it a block total read from an AL-FEC message ( Section 12.2; Section 12); the check of -00, unscoped, fired on a conforming append. Within a consumer protected under a flow of the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2, governed for its blocks or not, the packet that anchors the check and the packet it tests are ones that profile admitted, so a symbol of an unlisted track delivered over a MoQ unicast path neither anchors nor trips it, and one below a held layer's bound is discarded. A receiver that joins a withdrawn highest layer under a catalog that still lists it is caught only where a block generated while the layer was published reaches it and it holds a layer below, and otherwise learns of the withdrawal at the next catalog refresh, which Section 6.3.9 now states. Under Reed-Solomon a receiver also checks SSB_length + RSB_length against 255.
Section 7.3: sub-blocks are described as defines them, and no session this document targets carries an OTI, so none uses them.
Section 8.5: is cited as a reference, and A3SA is the ATSC 3.0 Security Authority.
Sections 11 and 11.1: TreeDN is native SSM plus AMT relays, and the repair is generated end to end. Section 11 cites Sections 1 and 3 for TreeDN and the delivery paths.
Section 11.4.5: a keyframe repair FETCH has a lower SUBSCRIBER_PRIORITY number than every repair-track subscription the receiver holds on the session.
Sections 6.1 and 13: BCP 14 keywords are no longer used for a naming convention or in an informative section.

Sections 7.6.5, 12 and 14.4: no requirement rests on an informative reference. Secure Objects and Common Encryption are examples, and the ATSC 3.0 ingest guidance sets no requirement of its own: the one BCP 14 keyword in Section 12 restates the status Section 4.3 gives "raptorq".
Section 14.3: the overhead bound applies by default to layer 0 of the base instance, since further layers are added on demand.
Section 14.4: deployments that authenticate packets need a mechanism that covers the FEC Payload IDs; version 2 of the bc-provenance profile does.

Sections 5.1 and 15: the algorithm registry carries the catalog identifier and gives guidance to the designated expert, and a new "MoQ FEC Block Profiles" registry (Section 15.4) holds the blockProfile values.

Sections 4.5, 5.1, 5.1.2, 7.6.7 and Appendix B: the catalog examples carry the mandatory fields version, isLive and bitrate. In Section 7.6.7 interleaveDepthMs is 1200, which covers the block's send span.
References: is normative, since Sections 6.3.6 and 11.4 set requirements on its endpoints and legs. Added , and as informative and as normative.

Sections 8.5, 11.3 and 14.4 name version 2 of the bc-provenance profile of Section 7.2, whose digest covers the Source FEC Payload ID of source packets and the Repair FEC Payload ID of repair packets. Section 11.3 item 3 describes a per-object scheme that authenticates every multicast symbol before it enters the decoder and checks a recovered packet against its own digest or withholds it.

Section 7.4 states that, within a consumer the bc-provenance profile governs for its blocks (one protected under a flow whose endpoint lists its source track; one a repair-only endpoint feeds while the source track comes over MoQ unicast alone is outside the profile for Sections 7.4, 9 and 11.4), a block delimited only by symbols of an unlisted track (one that no endpoint of a flow the consumer is protected under lists: one no multicast endpoint the receiver holds lists, holding being joined to its group, reading its manifest track or receiving the broadcast that carries the flow, or one a held endpoint lists while the consumer is not yet protected under its flow) is provisional and yields to an admitted repair packet that conflicts with it, as Section 7.2.7 specifies, the fail-closed rule then applying among admitted packets, and that such symbols reveal no run of lost SS_IDs. Section 6.3.6 states that a consumer is protected under an endpoint's flow only while the receiver holds the endpoint.

Sections 9 and 11.4 state that, within such a consumer, a symbol of an unlisted track enters a decode only as step 2 of Section 7.2.7 allows, which bounds the decodes a block takes with such symbols' help, that a source symbol the profile has not admitted is not held in deciding whether a block is unrecovered at its FEC deadline, that the packet whose receipt anchors a block's ts is the first packet of the block, in receipt order, that the profile admits, whenever it admits it, never such a symbol, that a block only such symbols have delimited is held for decoding only, with no ts and no FEC deadline whatever packets are admitted into or above its range, the SS_IDs it covers that the receiver lacks being runs of Section 11.4 as if it were not delimited, and that the open-block bound discards a block that has no ts before any block that has a ts; Section 7.5 states that, within such a consumer, such a block is never the S_prev of the Group range, only a block that a repair packet the profile has admitted delimits counting there; Section 14.4 item 4 sends a decode that fails an integrity check, and, within such a consumer, one whose recovered packets step 2 of Section 7.2.7 does not admit, to Section 11.4 instead of to the unicast fallback; Section 11.4.2 requests no repair for a block that reaches its deadline below a RAP the receiver has admitted complete, nor, within such a consumer, for a block only symbols of an unlisted track have delimited, which reaches no deadline, and Section 11.4.5 item 3 cancels no non-keyframe or audio repair at the deadline of a block Section 11.4.2 does not request.
Section 15.3: "MoQ Streaming Format" is now "MOQT Streaming Format", the name that uses.
